49 HSS - III Economics, Public Health Title Microeconomics-1 Number AIL4010 Department AIDE (CMCE) L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for B. Tech. Type Core for minor, Elective for all others Prerequisite None Objectives 1. Introduce the fundamental principles of individual decision-making. 2. Formalize the decision-making behavior for consumers as well as producers. 3. Set up the general equilibrium model and price determination. Learning Outcomes: 1. Understanding of axiomatic approach of economic decision-making. 2. Modeling economic decision -making in a tractable form and analyze the comparative - statics. 3. Understanding of basic market mechanisms and fundamentals behind price determination. Course Content: Preferences: axiomatic approach and examples. (4 lectures) Utility theory: representation theorem and examples. (4 lectures) Cardinal vs ordinal approaches. (3 lectures) Utility maximisation problem. (4 lectures) Demand analysis. (3 lectures) Expenditure minimisation problem as dual and Hicksian demand. (3 lectures) Integrability and recoverability (2 lectures) Weak axiom of revealed preference (3 lectures) Producer theory: profit maximisation and cost minimisation. (3 lectures) Welfare theorems (3 lectures) Market structures: Perfectly competitive market , Monopoly and discrimination (4 lectures) Strategic aspects in market structure: oligopoly (3 lectures) General equilibrium. (4 lectures) Reference Books: 1. A Short Course in Intermediate Microeconomics with Calculus. Feldman, A. & Serrano, R. , CUP, 2018. 2. Microeconomic theory. Mas-colell, A., Whinston, M.D., Green, J. R., Oxford University Press, 1995. 3. A Course in Microeconomic Theory. David M. Kreps, Princeton University Press, 1990.

50 Title Microeconomics-2 Number AIL4XX0 Department/School AIDE (CMCE) L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for B. Tech (All Branches), P.G., Ph.D. Type Core for minor, Elective for others Prerequisite Microeconomics-1 Objectives 1. To introduce strategic interactions among the rational economic agents in the general equilibrium framework 2. To equip students with concepts from market design such as auction theory. 3. To provide a thorough analysis of general equilibrium theory. Learning Outcomes 1. In depth understanding of strategic interactions in various economic models. 2. Understanding of dual economic decision -making of rational agents in a general equilibrium setting. Course Content Game theory: normal form games, common knowledge assumption, strategies, Nash equilibrium, simultaneous move games and examples, games of perfect information, games of imperfect information. (5 lectures) Information economics: adverse selection and moral hazard problems, examples, information and market performance. (12 lectures) Auctions and mechanism design problems. (13 lectures) General equilibrium theory: Debreu’s axiomatic approach to characterize equilibrium in competitive market - existence, uniqueness and stability; core and equilibria. (1 2 lectures) Reference Books: 1. Microeconomic theory, Mas-colell, A., Whinston, M.D., Green, J. R., OUP, 1995. 2. Theory of value: an axiomatic analysis of economic equilibrium, Debreu, G., Cowles Foundation, 1977. 3. Game theory, Fudenberg, D., Tirole, J., MIT Press, 1991. 4. Advanced microeconomic theory, Jehle, G.A., Reny, P.J., Pearson, latest edition. Online Course Material: 1. https://online.stanford.edu/courses/soe-ycs0004-game-theory-ii-advanced-applications

51 Title Health Economics Number HSL4070 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0[3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objective 1. To be able to evaluate the health sector in India using economic tools. 2. To have a global perspective and a broad understanding of institutional changes currently in the Indian healthcare system. Learning Outcomes 1. Understand microeconomic concepts and their application for the health sector. 2. Understand the role of economic incentives, competition and regulation on the functioning of the health care system. 3. Understand the health care insurance sector and financing of health care. 4. Understand how different healthcare systems function around the world. Contents Introduction to health economics: An introduction to health, health care, health system and health economics (5 lectures). Microeconomic and statistical concepts : Demand, supply, elasticity, production, market structures, economic efficiency & cost-benefit analysis, economic evaluation, and valuation of human life, regression analysis, statistical inference (12 lectures). Supply and Demand for health : Health production function and cost of health care, health demand, human capital model and the determinants of demand for healt h, demand for and supply of health insurance, uncertainty, adverse selection and moral hazard in the health insurance market (10 lectures). Healthcare Industry: Market Structure of health care industry, types and characteristics of various health care providers, India’s healthcare system (5 lectures). Government and Health care systems : Healthcare financing, rationale for government intervention in health care market and the nature of intervention by government in health care sector, Comparison of healthcare systems in different countries, Universal Health Coverage in India (10 lectures). Reference Books 1. Introduction to health economics. Guinness, & Wiseman. McGraw-Hill Education (UK), 2011. 2. McPake, B., Normand, C., Smith, S., & Nolan, A. (2020). Health economics: an international perspective. Routledge. 3. The Economics of Health and Health Care, Sherman Folland, Pearson, 7/e, 2012 4. Health Economics for Developing Countries: A Practical Guide , Witter S, T Ensor, M Jowett, and R Thompson, McMillan Education Ltd, 2000 Electronic Resource http://www.healtheconomics.com/resources/

52 Title Industrial Organisation Number HSL7XX0 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. To familiarise students with fundamental concepts used for economic analysis of firm behavior. 2. To equip the students with knowledge of benchmark models and strategic interactions. 3. To introduce students to varied applications of theoretical models. Learning Outcomes 1. A detailed understanding of various market structures and their implications for firms and consumers. 2. Ability to formally analyze firm behavior from an economic and strategic perspective. 3. Knowledge and understanding of important models and observable applications. Contents 1. Introduction to concepts for economic analysis: what is industrial organisation , overview of theoretical and empirical perspectives, law of diminishing marginal returns, demand function, cost function, profit maximization. (7 lectures) 2. Market structures and strategic techniques: perfect competition, monopolistic competition and monopoly, market power, efficiency and public policy, firms as strategic agents and Nash equilibrium. (7 lectures) 3. Price discrimination: perfect price discrimination, multi-market price discrimination, arbitrage and screening, non-linear pricing. (6 lectures) 4. Static and Dynamic competition: Bertrand paradox and capacity constraints, Cournot model, concentration indices, static approach to dynamic pricing, repeated interaction and collusion, price rigidities and excess capacity. (7 lectures) 5. Non-price competition : advertising, market power, information, R&D and innovation. (3 lectures) 6. Product differentiation: spatial competition models, advertising and information, vertical differentiation. (5 lectures) 7. Entry, accomodation and exit: natural monopoly and barriers to entry, stackelberg competition and applied strategies for deterrence. (5 lectures) 8. Network effects, auctions, strategic policy commitment and international trade. (2 lectures) Textbooks 1. Jeffrey Church and Roger Ware (2000), Industrial Organization: A S trategic Approach, McGraw Hill. 2. Jean Tirole (1998). The Theory of Industrial Organization, MIT Press. 3. Luis Cabral (2000) Industrial Organization: An Introduction, MIT Press. 4. Lynne Pepall, Dan Richards and George Norman (2014). Contemporary Theory and Empirical Applications, Wiley. 5. Xavier Vives (1999). Oligopoly Pricing: Old Ideas and New Tools , MIT Press. Reference books: 1. Anindya Sen (1996). Industrial organization, Oxford University Press. 2. Richard Schmalensee and R. Willig (1989). Handbook of Industrial Organization , vol. 1-2, 1 ed., Elsevier. 3. Mark Armstrong and Robert Porter (2007). Handbook of Industrial Organization, vol. 3, 1 ed., Elsevier. Research papers 1. Spence, A., (1976), Product Differentiation and Welfare , American Economic Review , 66, issue 2, p. 407-14. 2. Dixit, Avinash, (1986), Comparative Statics for Oligopoly, International Economic Review, 27, issue 1, p. 107-22. 3. Maskin, Eric and Riley, John, (1984), Monopoly with Incomplete Information , RAND Journal of Economics, 15, issue 2, p. 171-196. 4. d'Aspremont, Claude, Gabszewicz, Jean and Thisse, Jacques, (1979), On Hotelling's "Stability in Competition", Econometrica, 47, issue 5, p. 1145-50.

54 Title Health and Development Number HSL4XX0 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. To understand the relation between economic development and health status across the world in the modern period. 2. To understand the social and environment determinants of health and their relationship to economic policy. 3. To introduce equity as a dimension of progress towards universal health care and the sustainable development goals. 4. To understand the impact of globalization on the wellbeing of the world. Learning Outcomes 1. Understand the impact of economic development on the wellbeing of the world. 2. Appreciate economic growth and origins of inequality. 3. Conceptually understand the inequalities in health and role of social determinants. Contents Introduction to basic concepts of health and development: Health, illness and diseases, medicine, birth rate, death rate, life expectancy, mortality, morbidity, communicable and non -communicable diseases, gross domestic product, gross national income, huma n development, political economy of health and development (10 lectures). Wellbeing of the world: Different measures of wellbeing, health status in the modern world, life - expectancy, happiness index, and human development (7 lectures). Inequalities in hea lth, and social determinants of health: Social determinants of health; The Rio Declaration on Social determinants of health, health disparities, unequal access and utilisation of health services, trends in global poverty and income inequality (7 lectures). Impact of globalization on health: Five ways in which globalization affects health care -, structural adjustment programme and health, global institutions, impacts on environment, nature of work, financialization: neoliberalism and healthcare (7 lectures). Health, Development and Challenges in India: Understanding the current inter -linkages between health and development; poverty, health and development in India; main challenges in achieving the health-SDGs in India; widening inequalities in health status of population, low investment in public health services, shortages of human resources and medicines (10 lectures). Text Books : 1. WHO. (2008). Closing the gap in a generation: health equity through action on the social determinants of health - Final report of the commission on social determinants of health. 2. Deaton, A. (2013). The great escape: health, wealth, and the origins of inequality. Princeton University Press. 3. Marmot, M. (2015). The health gap: the challenge of an unequal world. Bloomsbury Publishing USA. Reference Books/Reports: 1. World Health Organization. (2001). Macroeconomics and health: investing in health for economic development. 2. Birn, A. E., Pillay, Y., & Holtz, T. H. (2017). Textbook of global health. Oxford University Press. 3. Balabanova, D., McKee, M., & Mills, A. (2011). Good health at low cost’25 years on what makes a successful health system?. 4. Johnson, S. A. (2017). Challenges in health and development: from global to community perspectives. Springer. Online Course Material https://www.coursera.org/learn/social-determinants-of-health

55 Title Indian Economic Development and Policy Number HS7XX Department HSS Structure (L-T-P-C) 3-0-0 Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives: The Instructor will: 1. Introduce students to current and evolving policy debates in the backdrop of issues pertaining to economic development of India. 2. Familiarize students with economic development issues and policy aspects which are important in professions involving nation -building broadly and policy formulation and implementation specifically. Able to have a broad perspective of the multifaceted nature of economic development issues and incorporate this in their professional pursuits. 56 Title Political and Institutional Economics of Development Number HSL7460 Department HSS Structure L-T-P (C) 3-0-0 (3) Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives: The Instructor will: As the economy is embedded in society, economic interactions and decisions are shaped and constrained by its framework of institutions, be it the state, individuals, formal laws or social norms. Economic development therefo re, is inevitably and intricately linked with, and determined by political economy, social norms and institutions. It is this idea that this course explores. Learning Outcomes: The students are expected to have the ability to: -Appreciate the importance of institutions, politics and society in economic growth and development -Appreciate the importance of the impact of intricately -related institutional and political aspects on individual decisions and actions, society and the economy. Contents: Institutions: Essence of Institutional Economics, Role of Institutions in Growth and Development, Varieties of Capitalism, Institutional Political Economy State, Law and Economy: Economic Role of Political Institutions, State Actors, Issues in Law and Economics Social Norms, Beliefs, Culture and Preferences: Role of social norms in individual preferences and economic outcomes, Role of Beliefs in Decision-making, Culture and Development Issues in Political Economy: Economics of Bureaucracy, Corruption, Media, Elections, Policies, 2008 Crisis, Bankruptcy Law Conflict: Economic Causes and Consequences of Democracy, Violence, Cooperation, War Selected Readings (will be revised periodically): 1.Acemoglu, D., Johnson, S., & Robinson, J. A. (2005). Institutions as a Fundamental Cause of Long-run Growth. Handbook of Economic Growth. Elsevier 2.Chang, H. J. (2011). Institutions and economic development: theory, policy and history. Journal of institutional economics 3.Engerman and Sokoloff (2000). History Lessons: Institutions, Factors Endowments, and Paths of Development in the New World. Journal of Economic Perspectives 4.Weingast, B. R. (1995). The Economic Role of Political Institutions: Market-preserving Federalism and Economic Development. (Eds.). (2013). Law and Economics: Volume I: Theory, Volume II: Practice. SAGE Publications India. 10.Bardhan, P. (2004). 57 Title Foundations of Finance Number HSL4XX0 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Prerequisite None Objectives 1. The course will help students to acquire breadth of knowledge of the various segments in financial markets. 2. Introduce the functioning of Banking and financial market structure 3. This course aims at providing the students the intricacies of Indian financial system for better financial decision making. 4. This course will address many critical personal financial management topics in order to help students to learn prudent habits both while in college and throughout lifetime. Through this course, the stu dents will cover a variety of personal finance topics, including budgets, investing, and managing risk. Learning Outcomes 1. Students will develop an in depth understanding of the linkages and the interconnected nature of the global currency, bond, commodity and equity markets. 2. Students will understand the importance of Indian financial system in the economic development of the country as it encourages both savings and investment 3. This course will teach students on how to master their money, how to gr ow income, reduce debt, budget the smart way, invest money, and manage taxes and not avoiding them. Contents Module 1: Basics of Money, Banking and Financial Markets: An overview of the Financial System, Money; Understanding Interest rates and its behav ior, Central Banks and the Federal Reserve System, Money Supply Process, The stock market, The theory of rational expectations, and the efficient market hypothesis, An economic analysis of the financial structure and regulation, Financial Crises in advanced economies, Financial Crises in emerging economies, Banking and Management of Financial Institutions, Basics of Indian Financial System, Trends and Progress on Banking, RBI, SEBI and NSE India Annual Reports, Discussion on World Development Report and IMF report (16 lectures) Module 2: How Finance Works: Financial Analysis, Financial Perspective, Source of value creation, The art and science of valuation, Capital allocation (16 lectures) Module 3: Personal Finance Basics: Personal Finance, Saving Money for the future, Managing Debt, Fundamentals of Investing, Risk management in personal finance, Personal Tax Management (10 lectures) Textbook 1. Mishkin, F.S. 2019. The economics of Money, Banking and Financial Markets. 10th edition. Pearson India. Other Reference Books 1. Machiraju, ‘Indian Financial System’ – Vikas Publishing House, 2nd Edition, 2002. 2. Varshney P.N., & Mittal D.K., ‘Indian Financial System’, Sultan Chand & Sons, New Delhi. 2002. Online Resources 1. Prof. Abhijeet Chandra, Behavioral and Pe rsonal Finance, https://nptel.ac.in/courses/110/105/110105144/ 2. Prof. Jitendra Mahakud, Introduction to Financial System, https://nptel.ac.in/courses/110/105/110105121/

58 Title Individual and strategic decision making: theory and applications Number AIL4XX0 Department AIDE (CMCE) L-T-P [C] 2-0-0 [2] Offered for UG and PhD Type Core for minor, Elective for others Prerequisite None Exclusions Introduction to game theory MAL4310 Objectives 1. Introduce students to the fundamentals of game theory and strategic behaviour. 2. To provide a formal and intuitive understanding of solution concepts in game theory. 3. To equip students with knowledge of simultaneous and extensive form games. 4. To familiarise students with economic and behavioral applications of game theory. Learning Outcomes: 1. Understanding of fundamentals of game theory: game forms, strategies, equilibrium notions, rationalizability, solution concepts and techniques. 2. Students will be able to model strategic behaviour in various economic settings. 3. Students will be equipped with formal knowledge of solution concepts and techniques wh ich have broad applications for problem solving in various strategic settings. Course Content: Introduction to strategic games (2 lectures) Strict and weak domination (2 lectures) Rationalizability and iterated elimination (4 lectures) Nash equilibrium (3 lectures) Pure and mixed strategies (3 lectures) Correlated equilibrium and strategies (1 lectures) Bayesian games and Bayesian equilibrium (2 lectures) Extensive form games (2 lectures) Games of perfect and imperfect information (2 lectures) Backward induction procedure (2 lectures) Repeated games: finite and infinite (3 lectures) Folk theorems (2 lectures) Reference Books: 1. Martin J. Osborne and Ariel Rubinstein, "A Course in Game Theory", MIT Press (1994). 2. Drew Fudenberg and Jean Tirole, "Game Theory", MIT Press (1991). 3. Michael Maschler, Ellon Solan and Shmuel Zamir, "Game Theory", CUP (2013). Online Resources: 1. Game Theory, SOE -YCS4002 Stanford School of Engineering. https://online.stanford.edu/courses/soe-ycs0002-game-theory

59 Title Social and Economic Networks Number AIL7XX0 Department/School AIDE (CMCE) L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for B. Tech./PG/Ph.D. Type Elective Prerequisite Individual and strategic decision making: theory and applications Objectives: 1. To introduce students to formal methods of modeling formation and evolution of networks. 2. To provide conceptual understanding of applications of network theory to social and economic problems. 3. To provide knowledge of benchmark models. Learning outcomes: 1. Students will be equipped to model and analyze a wide variety of social and economic networks. 2. Students will gain an understanding of key concepts and important models. 3. Students will be familiar with the tools required for strategic analysis of networks. Course content: Introduction to networks: need for modeling networks, applications in economics and society. (3 lectures) Representing and measuring networks: nodes, players and graphs; types of networks; degree and density; degree distribution; clustering; cliquishness; centrality. (7 lectures) Random networks: Poisson networks; Markov graphs; Expected degree model etc.; properties of random networks. (8) Network games: stability; efficiency; diffusion and learning; strategic in teractions and network structure; equilibria notions; dynamic behavior and contagion. (16) Economic applications: trade; information transmission and beliefs; public goods; influence etc. (9 lectures) Reference Books: 1. Matthew O. Jackson, "Social and Economic Networks", Princeton University Press (2008). 2. Gabrielle Demange and Myrna Wooders Eds. “Group Formation in Economics Networks, Clubs, and Coalitions”, Cambridge University Press (2005). 3. Bhaskar Dutta and M atthew O. Jackson Eds. “Networks and Groups: Models of Strategic Formation”, Studies in Economic Design, Springer (2003). Research papers: 1. Galeotti, A., Sanjeev Goyal, M. O. Jackson, Fernando Vega -Redondo, and Leeat Yariv. "Network Games." The Review of Economic Studies 77, no. 1 (2010): 218-44. 2. Jackson, M.O. "Allocation Rules for Network Games,'' Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 51, Issue 1, April 2005, Pages 128-154. Online resources: “Social and Economic Networks: Models and Analysis”, SOHS -YECON0001, Stanford School of Humanities and Social Sciences. https://online.stanford.edu/courses/sohs-yecon0001-social-and- economic-networks-models-and-analysis

60 Title Behavioral Economics and Decision theory Number AIL7XX0 Department/School AIDE (CMCE) L-T-P [C] 3-0-0[3] Offered for B. Tech./P.G./Ph.D. Type Elective Prerequisite Microeconomics-1 Objectives: 1. To familiarise students with standard models of individual decision-making. 2. To equip students with different modeling techniques. 3. To provide an overview of current literature in bounded rationality and it's intersections with AI. Learning Outcomes: 1. Knowledge of fundamentals of decision theory and modeling techniques. 2. A deep understanding of bounded rationality and formal approaches for modeling behavioral phenomena. 3. Development of conceptual understanding required for application of decision theoretic models and framework to various relev ant settings such as online e -retailing, search algorithms, etc. Course Content: Rational choice: binary relations, preference orderings, representation theorems (7 lectures) Important axioms in choice theory, their relevance in characterizing choice and underlying behavioral intuition: WARP, GARP, Independence axioms etc. (7 lectures) Decision theory models with boundedly rational agents: imperfect attention, cognitive constraints, attribute based models, framing effects, etc. (7 lectures) Stochastic choice models: random utility model, Luce rule, two-stage decision making etc. (6 lectures) Decision-making under uncertainty: subjective probabilities, V -N-M theorem, de -Finetti's theorem, Savage's theorem, Anscombe-Aumann framework. (9 lectures) Applications of decision theory in AI: list-based decision making models and online search, e-retailing platforms, stop-and-choose decision rules, attention and online advertising etc. (7 lectures) Reference Books: 1. David M. Keeps, "Notes on the Theory of Choice", Westview Press (1988). 2. Itzhak Gilboa, "Theory of Decision under Uncertainty", CUP (2009). 3. Paul Anand, Prasanta Pattanaik and Clemens Puppe, "The Handbook of Rational and Social Choice", OUP (2009). 4. Ariel Rubinstein, "Modeling Bounded Rationality", MIT Press (1998). 5. Ran Spiegler, "Bounded Rationality and Industrial Organisation", OUP (2018).

62 Title Fundamentals of Logic Number HSL4010 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The main aims of the course are: (1)Learning effective methods to solve a variety of disagreements. (2)Obtaining the ability to identify different types of arguments and evaluating them (3)Obtaining the ability to translate ordinary language into logical language Learning Outcomes (1)Developing the ability to prove valid arguments by using different methods of proof. (2)Realizing that proper use of logic is an effective and reasonable way in resolving disagreements. Contents Introduction: Nature, scope and history of logic, various types of arguments, validity, truth and soundness, complexity of natural language, symbolization. Propositional Logic: truth functions, truth tables, indirect truth tables, rules of implication, rules of replacement, indirect proof, conditional proof. Syllogistic Logic: categorical propositions, quality, quantity, distribution, traditional square of opposition, Venn diagrams and modern square of opposition, conversion, obversion and contraposition, categorical syllogisms, mood and figure, rules and fallacies. Predicate Logic: symbols and translation, using rules of inference, change of quantifier ru le, conditional and indirect proof, relational predicates and identity. Reference Books: 1. Hurley, Patrick (2008) Introduction to Logic(India edition) Imprint, Wadsworth. 2. Copy, Irving (2006)Symbolic Logic Prentice-Hall of India, Pvt.Ltd. 3. Lepore, Ernest and Cumming Sam (2009)Meaning and Argument Wiley Blackwell.

63 Title Critical Thinking Number HSL4XXX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The Instructor will: 1 Help the students in developing the ability to think critically and cogently 3. Developing the ability to recognise fallacies and overcome them 3- Appreciate the recent developments in the study of cognition that shed light on how reason is fallible in everyday life. Learning Outcomes 1.Knowing 'how to think' and not just 'what to think' 2. A critical mind set which includes being self critical 3. Developing qualities like inquisitiveness, open mindedness and intellectual honesty. Lecture Modules/Contents: 1. introduction : The difference between normal thinking and critical thinking, Reason and its applications, The need for critical thinking(5 lectures) Empirical evidence for improvement in critical thinking, Marks of a critical thinker, Four-Part Model for critical thinking (5 lectures) Cognitive Illusions:: Illusions of thinking: conjunction fallacy, confirmation bias, base rates in Bayesian inference, illusory correlation, illusory control. Biases in deductive reasoning, Illusions of judgement: availability, representativeness, anchoring effect, validity effect, (5 lectures) Illusions of memory: Moses illusion, orientation illusion, associative illusion, misinformation effect, hindsight bias, illusions of change or stability(5 lectures) Fallacies in everyday reasoning : Fallacies of Relevance: appeal to force, appeal to pity, appeal to people, argument against the person, red derring, straw man, missing the point.(5 lectures) Fallacies of Weak Induction: Appeal to unqualified authori ty, appeal to ignorance, hasty generalisation, false cause, slippery slope, weak analogy, Fallacies of Presumption:begging the question, complex question, false dichotomy, amphiboly, composition and division (6 lectures) Modeling Cognition: Two systems,Ada ptive Unconscious , Evolutionary Reasons, Dolphin Model of cognition(5 lectures) Practical lessons : Diagnosing fallacies, strategies to think without committing the fallacies.(5 lectures) Reference Books: 1. Cognitive Illusions (2012) Rudiger F. Pohl (ed) Psychology Press, New York 2. Critical Thinking: An Exploration of Theory and Pracise ( 2007)Jennifer Moon, Routledge. 3. Thought and Knowledge: An Introduction to Critical Thinking (2013)Diane Halpern. Psychology Press. 4. An Introduction to Critical Thinking(2010) Madhucchanda Sen. Pearson Online Resource https://www.reasoninglab.com/

64 Title Cognitive Semantics Number 32209/HSL4xxx Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. To provide an overview of the field of cognitive semantics which tries to explain the phenomenon of linguistic meaning as part of overall cognitive capacities. 2. To explore the basis of ingrained assumptions concerning meaning, reason, imagination and understanding Learning Outcomes 1.Understanding how linguistic capacity can arise out of overall cognitive capacities. 2. Understanding how metaphors are all -pervasive in our lives and the need to revisit many of the metaphors used in day to day conceptualisations Course Contents Introduction: Guiding principles, Generalisation commitment and cognitive commitment. Phenomena investigated within cognitive semantics,methodology and comparison with formal semantics (6 lectures) Embodiment: Image schemas and their properties, list of image schemas and their relation with abstract thought, conceptual structure(6 lectures) Encyclopaedic view of meaning: word meaning versus sentence meaning, frame semantics, theory of domains (6 lectures) Categorisation and Idealised Cognitive Models : Prototype theory, Idealised Cognitive Models.(6 lectures) Metaphor and Metonymy: Conceptual Metaphor Theory, Primary Metaphor Theory, Conceptual Metonymy(6 lectures) Meaning Construction: Cognitive theory of meaning construction, the architecture of mental space construction, the dynamic nature of meaning construction (6 lectures) Reference Books 1. Evans, Vyvyan and Green Melaine(2006) Cognitive Linguistics: An Introduction Edinburg University Press 2. Johnson, Mark (1987)Body in the Mind: The bodily basis of Meaning, Imagination and Reason , University of Chicago Press. 3. Lakoff, George and Johnson, Mark(199) Philosophy in the Flesh Basic Books. 4. Talmy, L (2003)Towards a Cognitive Semantics MIT Press.

67 Title Theories of Justice Number HSL4xx0 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0[3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The course will: 1. Introduce major philosophical positions on justice 2. Present the role of justice in diverse contexts of sociopolitical life Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Understand the philosophical foundations of the concept of justice 2. Evaluate the present social order and envision a just social structure Contents Justice: Early Notions: Hellenistic tradition: Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle; the principle of harmony and order; major religious traditions; Indian tradition Justice in Utilitarian View: consequentialism; the idea of greatest welfare; balancing individual happiness and social welfare; major thinkers and seminal works Justice in Libertarian Position: role of liberty of individuals; rights and limits of the state; positive and negative liberty; classical and contemporary libertarian thinkers; merits and limitations of libertarian position Justice in Egalitarian View: equality and egality; idea of fairness; capabilities and dignity; concept of equal opportunity; major philosophers and works Justice in Contractualist Framework: justice being determined by the terms of contracts; the centrality of freedom; major thinkers and works; limitations of the contractualist position Applied Areas: distributive justice; procedural justice; international justice; intergenerational Justice; restorative justice Reference Books 1. 70 Title Disaster risk reduction and management Number HSL4030 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite Interest in Policy, Governance, Sustainability, Law, Gender or Interdisciplinary/cross- discipline background Objectives The Instructor will: 1. Provide an overview of the conceptual and critical understanding on policy measures on disaster governances. 2. Introduce students to examine the role of decentralization of disaster resources and responsibilities, and best practice principles in preparedness, mitigatio n, response, recovery and reconstruction. 3. Facilitate the students to understand the how disasters impact societies. Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Interpret the theories and concepts underlying the principles and practices of disaster risk reduction and management. 2. Develop the capacity to participate in debates on disaster governance and societal reconstruction. 3. By the end of the course, students will be able to understand the disaster resilience, risk mitigation, and recovery policies. Contents Introduction on Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRR&M) across space and time : (2 lectures) Definition and types of disaster: hazards and disasters, risk and vulnerability in disasters, natural and man-made disasters (6 lectures) Risk management: nature, technocracy, and behavioural governance (4 lectures) Paradigm shifts in DRR&M: policy & governance issues, UN Agenda (5 lectures) Social and economic impact of disasters: class, communities and societies, disaster capitalism (6 lectures) Gender and disaster: Feminist discourse (4 lectures) Rights and justice: humanitarian aid and CSOs in DRR&M (3 lectures) Mitigation and Management techniques of Disaster: basic principles of disasters management, disaster management cycle, national and state bodies for disaster management (6 lectures) Community-based disaster risk management discourse analyses: ‘bottom-up’ approaches’, community innovations (3 lectures) Disaster and Development Research: A way forward (2 lectures) Textbook: A handbook with all the study material will be given to the students. Reference Books 1. Wisner B., Blaikie P., Cannon T. & Davis I., (2004), At risk: natural hazards, people’s vulnerability and disasters, 2nd edn, London: Routledge. 2. UNSDR (2009). UNISDR terminology on disaster risk reduction. United Nations International Strategy for Disaster Reduction (UNISDR): Switzerland, Geneva. Online Course Material 1. Pasupuleti, R.M., Disaster Recovery and Build Back Better, NPTEL Course Material, Indian Institute of Technology, Roorkee, https://nptel.ac.in/courses/124/107/124107010/

71 Title Political and Cultural Ecology Number HSL4xx0 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. The course will examine society-ecology relationships at different scales. 2. Provide a historical perspective to understand how past political and economic injustice in continuing environmental destruction. 3. To know the actors and actions involved in various processes of sustainable development Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Analyze how inequalities of power and wealth on different scales contribute to ecological imbalance 2. Critically analyze projects on sustainable development 3. Know historical inequalities and lasting legacy in form of environmental destruction Contents 1. What is Political and Cultural Ecology? Introduction to political ecology, its conceptual, historical and methodological origins - 10 2. Social Constructions of Nature – What is social construction of nature?, Political ecology and constructivists approaches to nature, social constructions and community management of natural resources - 5 3. Natural resource management and conservation – National parks, state -governed conservation, Rise of community based conservation and its critiques, critiques of different conservation techniques, Actors in conservation, Indian Context – 14 4. Development, Degradation and Marginalization – Explore relationship between development and marginalization of particular communities, study actors and institutions involved in the studies - 8 5. Neoliberalism and Environmental Governance – Neoliberalism and conservation, How do processes of neoliberalism affect ecology? Environmental management in a neo-liberal world – 5 Text Books : Robbins, P. (2012). Political Ecology: A Critical Introduction. Oxford: Blackwell:Wiley Reference Books: 1. Blaike, P. (1985). The Political Economy of Soil Erosion in Developing Countries. London: Longman 2. Harvey, D. (2003). The New Imperialism. Oxford: OUP 3. Vasan, S. (2006). Living with Diversity: Forestry Institutions in the Western Himalayas. IIAS: Shimla Online Course Material 1. http://janux.ou.edu. 2. https://www.politicalecology.eu/

76 Title Popular Classics Number HS 3xx Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The Instructor will: 1. Introduce students to a global canvas of popular classics in both literature and films. 2. Facilitate the students to understand a spectrum of values, experiences and ideas over the ages. 3. Contextualize literature and films in the context of global cultures, li teratures, movements and technologies Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Access enhanced creative and critical abilities, practice close reading, develop skills in structuring arguments and interpretations. 2. Create, engage and to build their personal narratives by creative interactions and discussions. 3. Reflect upon the diversity of cultures, values and creative practices from around the world and within the country Contents: Introduction – High Cultures and Popular Cultures Literary Devices and Elements of Fiction – Plot, Characters, Setting, Narration, Voices, Point of View, Conflict. Adaptations – Theories of Adaptations, Forms, Adapters, Contexts, Appeals, Audiences. 77 Title Introduction to Film Studies Number HSL2XXX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The instructor will: 1. Help students to explore the phenomenon of cinema as a scientific invention, as a cultural form and as a public institution 2. Help students to become familiar with some of the most significant events and movements in the history of transnational cinema 3. Introduce aesthetic, historical, cultural and political aspects of cinema and its mainstream and alternative histories in order to understand the medium as mass -culture as well as an experimental one Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Read film as a complex cultural/political/aesthetic text 2. Explore global film histories and (re)locate the cultural -cinematic history of the Indian nation-state within it 3. Develop acquaintance with concepts, theories and modes of writing on cinema, exploring English as well as non-English sources (in translation) Contents Introducing Cinema as an art form, early cinema, apparatus, sound and colo ur: Basic aspects of cinema and its history since the silent era Film movements, auteur, genre: Case studies (the Italian Neo -Realism/the French New Wave for movement, Western/Gangster/Film Noir as genre, Ray/Ghatak as auteur) Film criticism and cinematic writing: Criticism workshops, modes of writing (mimetic etc.), exploration of reading strategies Many Histories of Indian Cinemas: Histories of Bombay cinema and the city of Mumbai, Indian arthouse, fans, stars and cine-politics in South Indian cinemas The ‘other’ continents : Case studies (Latin American cinemas as a case study, with explorations of cinemas from Brazil and/or Argentina) Cinema and the Contemporary: The Age of the Digital, digital cinema and cinephilia, the transitional phase from the celluloid to the digital, copyright and piracy, introduction to new media theories, the changing exhibition space, audio-visual essays Textbooks 1. Bordwell, D., and Thompson, K., (2012), Film Art: An Introduction, McGraw-Hill. Reference Book 1. Martin, A., (2014), Mise en Scène and Film Style: From Classical Hollywood to New Media Art, Palgrave Macmillan. 2. Prasad, M. M., (2014), Cine-Politics: Film Stars and Political Existence in South India , Orient Blackswan. Online Course Material 1. http://sensesofcinema.com/category/great-directors/

78 Title Dalit Movement and Literature Number HSL7xx0 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The instructor will: 1. Help students to explore the intricacies of concepts such as nation and nationalism, caste, caste oppression, and caste as an exercise of power 2. Help students to become familiar with theorizations on dalits and untouchability, alternative/non-normative histories of nation, literature and culture 3. Make students familiar with the vast corpus of dalit literature that challenges the hierarchical mode of existing, standard-received histories of Indian literature Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Develop a basic engagement with dalit movements, histories and literatures 2. Develop alternative ways and modes of reading existing literary and cultural histories 3. Develop a theoretically nuanced understanding of ‘difference’ and ‘exceptionalism’ in the literature of the oppressed Contents Introducing the Dalit: Dalit as opposed to ‘Harijan’, Reading Ambedkar, Phule and others, critique of the Gandhian thought on the lower-caste, the Gandhi-Ambedkar debate (10 lectures) The Old and the New: Critique of the more traditional schools of dalit criticism such as the works of D. R. Nagaraj and others, reading histories of movements such as the dalit panther and their manifesto, philosophical exploration of untouchability as manifested in Aniket Jaaware’s works (10 lectures) Literatures and Challenges: Dalit modernity, dalits in and after the 1990s, dalit autobiographies, challenging the canonical literatures, identity politics and writing (10 lectures) Literary instances: Dalit writings from Eastern India (Adwaita Mallabarman), Western India (Marathi writings of Baburao Bagul, Sharankumar Limbale), and Southern India (G. Kalyana Rao, Challapalli Swaroopa Rani, B. Krishnappa, Siddalingaiah, Devanoora Mahadeva, Bama, C. Ayyappan et al.) (12 lectures) Textbooks 1. Satyanarayana, K., and Tharu, S., (eds.) (2013), The Exercise of Freedom: An Introduction to Dalit Writing, Navayana. 2. Jaaware, A., (2018), Practicing Caste: On Touching and Not Touching , Orient Blackswan. 3. Satyanarayana, K., and Tharu, S., (eds.) (2011), No Alphabet in Sight: New Dalit Writing from South India, Dossier I: Tamil and Malayalam, Penguin. 4. Satyanarayana, K., and Tharu, S., (eds.) (2013), From those Stubs, Steel Nibs are Sprouting: New Dalit Writing from South India, Dossier II: Kannada and Telugu , HarperCollins. Reference Book 1. Rege, S., (ed.) (2006), Writing Caste, Writing Gender: Narrating Dalit Women’s Testimonies, Zubaan. 2. Dangle, A., (ed.) (1992), Poisoned Bread: Translations from Modern Marathi Dalit Literature, Orient Longman. Online Course Material NPTEL course on caste in Indian English fiction is available at: https://nptel.ac.in/courses/109/106/109106135/

79 Title Cine-Politics under the National Emergency Number HSL7330 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The instructor will: 1. Help students to explore the intricacies of cultural forms and practices in the larger context of the political lives of the Indian nation 2. Help students to become familiar with some of the most significant events in the history of post-independence India through the prism of film history and state policy 3. 80 Title Perspectives in Language and Literary Studies Number DHL6010 Department IDRP: DH L-T-P-D [C] 3-0-0-1 [4] Offered for M.Sc. Introduce students to theories of literature. 2. Introduce students to basic theories of language, linguistics concepts, and literary cultures in translation. 3. Provide the students with a background in the development of computational tools for literary analysis Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Understand major trajectories in literary thought, trace the evolution of literary genres, and contextualize their contemporary significance. 2. Understand fundamental aspects of language and linguistic analysis. 3. Critically analyse literary texts using digital tools. 81 Title Introduction to Editing and Publishing Number HS7XX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0[3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The instructor will: 1. Provide an overview of a modern publishing industry, its history, and its various processes with special focus on the roles of editors 2. Equip the students with the practical skills and knowledge required to enter this industry Learning Outcomes Students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Perform the skills of basic editing and publishing as editors while also acquiring the knowledge of the language and tools of editing 2. Know and understand the processes of the industry that will prepare them for employability Contents Part Part 1: Overview 1. History of publishing (2 lectures) 2. Various kinds of publishing (2 lectures) 3. Structure and processes of and opportunities in a publishing house (2 lectures) 4. What is editing and what are the roles of an editor (2 lectures) 5. Difference between editing, copyediting, and proofreading (1 lectures) 6. The future of editing: online editing and its opportunities (1 lecture) Part 2: Understanding the editorial process 1. Commissioning manuscripts (1 lecture) 2. Working with writers (1 lecture) 3. Pre-editing or formatting (1 lecture) 2. Copyediting (1 lecture) 3. Proofreading (1 lecture) 4. Language of editing: The editing markups and style guides (2 lectures) 5. Tools of editing: Grammar and its various components (3 lectures) Part 3: The practice of editing Practical sessions on different for ms of editing and stages of the editorial process on different media: 1. Citations (print and electronic) 2. Hard-copy editing and editing on the screen 3. Working with MS Word (12 lectures) Part 4: Interaction with industry experts with focus on ethical and legal issues This may be in the form of internship opportunities, workshops, field visits, or guest lectures (10 lectures) Textbook 1. Chicago Manual of Style. 2017. 17th Edn. Chicago, Illinois: University of Chicago Press 2. Sabin, William A. The Gregg Reference Manual: A Manual of Style, Grammar, Usage, and Formatting. 2005. 10th Edn. New York, NY: McGraw-Hill/Irwin 3. Kesavan, Bellary Shamanna. 1985, 1988. History of Printing and Publishing in India: A Story of Cultural Re-awakening. 2 vol. New Delhi: National Book Trust 4. Butcher, Judith et al. Butcher's Copy-editing: The Cambridge Handbook for Editors, Copy-editors and Proofreaders. 2006. 4th edn. New York, NY: Cambridge UP 5. Devasar, Nitasha. Publishers On Publishing: Inside India’s Book Business 6. Gupta, Abhijit and Swapan Chakravorty. Print Areas: Book History in India 7. ---. Move-able Type: Book history in India Reference Books 1. Mackenzie, Janet. The Editor’s Companion . 2011. 2nd Edn. Cambridge University Press, Melbourne: Cambridge University Press

83 Title Indian Cinemas: Many Histories Number HSL7XX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The instructor will: 1. Help students in exploring the intricacies of historiography in general and film historiography in particular 2. Help students to become familiar with some of the most significant schools and modes of film history-writing in the context of India and its many cine-cultural industries 3. Make students familiar with conceptua l apparatuses in film history and their overlaps with national and global political and cultural histories Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Engage with complex discursive formulations in historiography 2. Explore associations between multiple histories of a specific site of inquiry 3. Develop acquaintance with contemporary scholarly writings on Indian film history, politics and cultural formations Contents What is Film History? : Readings on film history, many hist ories, historiographies, history -writing methods, contemporary history (4 lectures) Colonial Histories: Priya Jaikumar’s work on empire cinema, Lee Grieveson’s anthology on empire cinema (2 lectures) National Histories: Sumita S. Chakravarty’s work on Indian cinema and the nation-state (2 lectures) Ideological Histories : M. Madhava Prasad’s Marxist -ideological study, history of ideas and their textual-cinematic evidences (2 lectures) Institutional Histories : Peter Sutoris’ work on the Films Division, Sudh a Tiwari’s articles on FFC/NFDC, histories of the film society movement (2 lectures) The Biographical-Historical: M. S. S. Pandian’s work on M. G. Ramchandran, Theodore Baskaran’s biography of Sivaji Ganesan (1 lecture) Economic History: Ashish Rajadhyaksh a on Bombay industry’s illegitimacy, the underbelly of the city and its economy (2 lectures) History of Exhibition : S. V. Srinivas’ article on cinema hall and its public in South India, Adrian Athique on multiplex and the changing viewing practices (2 lectures) Global History: Ravi S. Vasudevan on global histories of Indian cinema, transnational cinema as method, Sudha Rajagopalan on the reception of Bombay cinema in the USSR, Nitin Govil’s narratives of encounter between Hollywood and Bombay (4 lectures) The Anthropological/Ethnographic: S. V. Srinivas on stardom, fan club and ethnographic research in Andhra Pradesh, Uma Bhrugubanda’s anthropological research on the citizen -devotee, Anand Pandian’s anthropological research on Tamil cinema (8 lectures) Genre Histories: Meheli Sen and Kartik Nair’s works on Indian horror films, Darshana Sreedhar Mini and Ratheesh Radhakrishnan on soft porn in South India/Kerala (3 lectures) Corporeal Histories: Usha Iyer’s recent work on dancing women, Meheli Sen & Anustup Basu’s edited book on figurations in Indian film (2 lectures) Spatial Historiography: Priya Jaikumar’s recent work on India as filmed space, Kaushik Bhaumik’s dissertation on Bombay’s urban history and cinema, Ranjani Mazumdar’s work on Bombay cinema and the city (8 lectures) Textbooks 1. Allen, R. C., and Gomery, D., (1985), Film History: Theory and Practice, Alfred A. Knopf. 2. Jaikumar, P., (2006), Cinema at the End of Empire: A Politics of Transition in Britain and India , Duke University Press. 3. Chakravarty, S. S., (1993), National Identity in Indian Popular Cinema 1947-1987, University of Texas Press.

85 Title Introduction to Literatures from India’s Northeast Number HSL7440 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0[3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The instructor will: 1. Introduce select texts from all eight states in India’s Northeast 2. Explain the context of each text 3. Focus primarily on novels, poems, and short stories with the exception of one song -text (to be read as a poem) Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Identify and understand at least one literary and one thematic issue from each text 2. Know about the heterogeneity of this forcefully homogenized and ‘invented’ region Contents Before We Begin: Understanding the Contexts 1. History of state formation: ‘Invented’ homogeneity and partition (3 lectures) 2. Culture of violence: ‘Disturbed’ area, AFSPA, nation and nationalism (2 lectures) 3. Introducing the eight states (1 lectures) Starting Out with the Texts 1. Mamang Dai’s The Legends of Pensam: The language question: the writer and her readers; Ecocritical concern through the Adi worldview (5 lectures) 2. Indira Goswami’s Pages Stained with Blood: The writer and the translation; The 1984 anti - Sikhs riots through an Assamese’s eyes (5 lectures) 3. ‘Miyah’/’Miya’ Poetry: Hafiz Ahmed’s “Write Down ‘I am a Miyah’”: The writer and his new language of protest; NRC and the ‘Na-Asamiya Muslims’ (2 lectures) 4. Mufidun Nisa’s “Wait, Flower, Don’t Bloom”: A Pangal writer in Manipur (Meitei) literary circle; The Meitei-Pangal clash of 1993 in Manipur (2 lectures) 5. Kshetrimayum Subadani’s “The Heat and the Agony”: ILP and the migrant workers in Manipur (2 lectures) 6. Esther Syiem’s Memoir in Water: Speaks the Wah Umkhrah: Oral culture in Syiem; Khasi matrilineal society (5 lectures) 7. Rokunga’s “ Ro Min Relsak Ang Che (Aw nang kan Lal kan Pathian )”: Mizo national consciousness in songs (2 lectures) 8. Mona Zote’s “An Impression of Being Alive”: The Korean influence in Mizo writing (2 lectures) 9. Temsula Ao’s “The Jungle Major” from These Hills Call Home: Stories from a War Zone : Narrating the collective; The Naga conflict (2 lectures) 10. Rajendra Bhandari’s Kshar/Akshar (“Perishable/Imperishable”): Nepali poetry of Sikkim; Ponderings on the ‘global in Gangtok’ (2 lectures) 11. Yishey Doma’s Legends of the Lepchas: Folk Tales from Sikkim : Agriculture/farming in Lepcha folktales (2 lectures) 12. Shefali Debbarma’s “Lamination”: Kokborok writing of Tripura; Identity politics: The dress and the Schedule Tribe (ST) card (2 lectures) Explorations: A Step Further (along with Starting Out with the Texts) 1. Author-centric criticism 2. Reader-centric criticism 3. Text-centric criticism 4. 85 Title Introduction to Literatures from India’s Northeast Number HSL7440 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0[3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The instructor will: 1. Introduce select texts from all eight states in India’s Northeast 2. Explain the context of each text 3. Focus primarily on novels, poems, and short stories with the exception of one song -text (to be read as a poem) Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Identify and understand at least one literary and one thematic issue from each text 2. Know about the heterogeneity of this forcefully homogenized and ‘invented’ region Contents Before We Begin: Understanding the Contexts 1. History of state formation: ‘Invented’ homogeneity and partition (3 lectures) 2. Culture of violence: ‘Disturbed’ area, AFSPA, nation and nationalism (2 lectures) 3. Introducing the eight states (1 lectures) Starting Out with the Texts 1. Mamang Dai’s The Legends of Pensam: The language question: the writer and her readers; Ecocritical concern through the Adi worldview (5 lectures) 2. Indira Goswami’s Pages Stained with Blood: The writer and the translation; The 1984 anti - Sikhs riots through an Assamese’s eyes (5 lectures) 3. ‘Miyah’/’Miya’ Poetry: Hafiz Ahmed’s “Write Down ‘I am a Miyah’”: The writer and his new language of protest; NRC and the ‘Na-Asamiya Muslims’ (2 lectures) 4. Mufidun Nisa’s “Wait, Flower, Don’t Bloom”: A Pangal writer in Manipur (Meitei) literary circle; The Meitei-Pangal clash of 1993 in Manipur (2 lectures) 5. Kshetrimayum Subadani’s “The Heat and the Agony”: ILP and the migrant workers in Manipur (2 lectures) 6. Esther Syiem’s Memoir in Water: Speaks the Wah Umkhrah: Oral culture in Syiem; Khasi matrilineal society (5 lectures) 7. Rokunga’s “ Ro Min Relsak Ang Che (Aw nang kan Lal kan Pathian )”: Mizo national consciousness in songs (2 lectures) 8. Mona Zote’s “An Impression of Being Alive”: The Korean influence in Mizo writing (2 lectures) 9. Temsula Ao’s “The Jungle Major” from These Hills Call Home: Stories from a War Zone : Narrating the collective; The Naga conflict (2 lectures) 10. Rajendra Bhandari’s Kshar/Akshar (“Perishable/Imperishable”): Nepali poetry of Sikkim; Ponderings on the ‘global in Gangtok’ (2 lectures) 11. Yishey Doma’s Legends of the Lepchas: Folk Tales from Sikkim : Agriculture/farming in Lepcha folktales (2 lectures) 12. Shefali Debbarma’s “Lamination”: Kokborok writing of Tripura; Identity politics: The dress and the Schedule Tribe (ST) card (2 lectures) Explorations: A Step Further (along with Starting Out with the Texts) 1. Author-centric criticism 2. Reader-centric criticism 3. Text-centric criticism 4. Context-centric criticism Textbook As mentioned in Starting Out with the Texts Reference Books An exhaustive list to be shared to interested students Online Course Materials The chapter titled “Writings in English from the Northeast: Reading Temsula Ao” from the NPTEL course Indian Fiction in English is available at: https://nptel.ac.in/courses/109/106/109106135/

86 Title Introduction to Contemporary Arts Number HS 4XX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The instructor will: 1. Introduce the world of visual art through a sneak peek into art histories and movements in India and in the world 2. Train the students to develop an eye for interpreting and understanding visual experiences and representations Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Appreciate different forms of creative and visual arts 2. Map histories of art movements in India and in the world 3. Understand and appreciate the aesthetic and philosophical aspects of visual representations Contents Introduction to visual arts with a focus on contemporary arts: Art, artwork, artworld (2 lectures) Pre-‘modern’ precedents: Art history and major art movements in the world (from classical to modern) (1 lecture) Histories of ancient and medieval Indian art: Styles of Mughal, Rajput, Pahari, and Southern India (1 lecture) Renaissance perspective and Indian resistance (1 lecture) Major ‘modern’ Indian artists and art groups: Colonized nation: Ravi Varma and the Bengal School; Amrita Sher -Gill and Indian modernist art; Rabindranath Tagore/Jamini Roy and Primitivism (6 lectures) Making (of) the nation : The Bombay artist: M F Hussain; Lahore art circle: Zubeida Agha; Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy: Zainul Abedin (6 lectures) Contesting (the) nation: Sudhir Patwardhan; Bikash Bhattacharjee’s hyper -realism; Khakhar’s ‘Pop’ art; Nalini Malani; Rokeya Sultana; Amruta Patil; Laishram Meena Devi (14 lectures) Representing the regions (of the nation): Folk art forms: Warli, Patachitra or Pattachitra, Kalamkari, Phad painting; Kalam (Kalamezhuthu); Tanjore painting; Madhubani painting (7 lectures) New modes of representation: Conceptual and performance arts (1 lecture) Experimental cinema (1 lecture) Installation art (1 lecture) New modes of exhibition: Digital art and exhibition (1 lecture) Textbooks 1. Mitter, Partha. Indian Art 1. Guha-Thakurta, Tapati. The Making of New Indian Art 2. Anand, Anand K, et al. Aesthetic Theories and Forms in Indian Tradition 3. Reiss, Julie H. From Margin to Center: The Spaces of Installation Art 4. Carrier, David. A World Art History and Its Objects 5. Bentkowska-Kafel,Anna. Digital Art History: A Subject in Transition 6. Chatterji, Roma. Speaking with Pictures: Folk Art and the Narrative Tradition in India 7. Gell, Alfred. “Vogel's Net: Traps as Artworks and Artworks as Traps.” The Art of Anthropology: Essays and Diagrams 8. Danto, Arthur. “The Artworld” 9. Becker, Howard. Art Worlds 10. Gombrich, Ernst. Art and Illusion 11. Arnheim, Rudolf. Art and Visual Perception Reference Book

88 Title Introduction to Performance Studies in India Number HS 7XX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The instructor will: 1. Introduce critical theoretical terms associated with performance studies in India 2. Provide an overview of various folk performative traditions in India 3. Explore the ‘political’ dimensions of these traditions Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Understand the difference between key theatrical terms in performance studies and aesthetics in the Indian context 2. Identify and know major moments in the history of performance linking various theatrical traditions with their unique practitioners 3. Get acquainted with the ‘politics’ of theatrical performance and aesthetics in India Contents Introduction to performance: Drama, script, theater/theatricality, performance/performativity, mimesis, presence, and materiality (2 lectures) Performance theories: Richard Schechner, Aparna Dhareshwar, Rustom Barucha, Erika Fischer- Lichte, and Marvin Carlson (5 lectures) Performance histories: In India and in the world (2 lectures) Traditions from the ‘other’ of India: Aristotle’s Poetics: The notion of the ‘plot’ (2 lectures) Brechtian ‘narration’ versus Aristotelian ‘plot/action’: Bertolt Brecht as background to ‘political’ performance practices (2 lectures) The Indian experiences: Bharata’s Natya Shastra and Kalidas’s Abhigyan Shakuntalam with focus on the rasa theory (abhinaya vs vritti) (3 lectures) Indian folk experiments: Utpal Dutt and Jatra, Habib Tanvir and Chhattisgarhi nacha, Girish Karnad and Yakshagana, Vijay Tendulkar and tamasha; Kathputli: the puppetry theatre of Rajasthan; Bhand Pather: the folk theatre of Kashm ir; Ratan Thiyam and performing the spectacle of the theatre of the root; Lai Haraoba festival of Manipur (16 lectures) The ‘other’ interventions: Binodini Dasi (performance in cinema), Manjula Padmanabhan’s Harvest and performance in/and the posthuman world; Heisnam Sabitri in Heisnam Kanhailal’s Draupadi (bodily performance), Swar Thounaojam and Bogey Systems (in English, Meiteilon, Kannada, and Tamil), and Mangai’s Frozen Fire and performing queer (10 lectures) Textbooks 1. Aristotle. Poetics 2. Schechner, Richard. Performance Studies and Performance Theory 3. Adorno, Theodor, et al. Aesthetics and Politics 4. Dharwadker, Aparna Bhargava. Theatres of Independence: Drama, Theory, and Urban Performances in India since 1947 5. Bharata. Natya Shastra 6. Fischer-Lichte, Erika, et al. The Routledge Introduction to Theatre and Performance Studies and The Transformative Power of Performance: A New Aesthetics 7. Hollander, Julia. Indian Folk Theatres 8. Bharucha, Rustom. Theatre and the World 9. ---. The Politics of Cultural Practice 10. ---. Terror and Performance 11. --- and Paula Richman (eds.). Performing the Ramayana Tradition (forthcoming) 12. Mukherjee, Tuntun. Staging Resistance: Plays by Women in Translation Reference Book 1. Wiles, D, and C Dymkowski (eds.). The Cambridge Companion to Theatre History

90 Title Modern Indian Theatre Number HSL7XX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The instructor will: 1. 1. Help students in exploring the intricacies of political and cultural histories of Indian theatre after the Indian Independence of 1947 2. 2. Make students familiar with the significance of many modes, forms and practices of theatre in the political lives of the Indian nation 3. 3. Help students to become familiar with some of the most significant events in the history of post- independence India through the prism of theatre, playwriting and playgoing Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. 1. Critically read playtexts and performance texts relevant for history-writing 2. 2. Explore associations between public institutions, postcolonial national history, mass, avant-garde and agit-prop theatre culture and the ever-changing socio-politico-cultural dynamics 3. 3. Develop acquaintance with contemporary scholarly writings on Indian theatre and politics Contents Post-Independence Statist Investment and Theatre Institutions: Legacies of IPTA & PWA, Nehruvian era and theatre policy in post -independence India, the formation of Sangeet Natak Akademi, National School of Drama, the language question, Theatre and Hindi public sphere, major directors and their legacy (3 lectures) Discourses around Theatre: The urban and the folk, politics of adaptation, Hindi theatre and regional theatre, politics of translation (3 lectures) Theatre in the long 1960s, Major Playwrights and their select plays : Mohan Rakesh ( Ashad ka Ek Din), Badal Sircar (Evam Indrajit), Vijay Tendulkar (Ghashiram Kotwal), Girish Karnad (Tuqlaq/The Fire and the Rain ), Mahesh Elkunchwar ( Garbo/Wada Chirebandi /Sonata/Aatmakatha), Komal Swaminathan ( Water! Water! ), H. Kanhailal ( Pebet), Satish Alekar ( Mahapoor/Begum Barve ), Chandrashekhar Kambar ( Jokumaraswami), K. N. Pa nikkar ( Karimkutty/The Lone Tusker ) (10 lectures) Production Histories: Works of directors such as Ebrahim Alkazi, Shombhu Mitra, Utpal Dutt, Vijaya Mehta, B. V. Karanth, Usha Ganguli, Ratan Thiyam (4 lectures) In Another Medium : Adaptations in cinema (Mani Kaul’s Ashad ka Ek Din , Yukt Film Collective’s Ghashiram Kotwal, Satyadev Dubey’s Shantata! Court Chalu Aahe) (6 lectures) The Exploration of the Folk : Readings on Habib Tanvir, reading of a select playtext ( Charandas Chor/Bahadur Kalarin) (3 lectures) Political Theatre/Third Theatre : Utpal Dutt’s Towards a Revolutionary Theatre , Badal Sircar’s writings on Third Theatre, Safdar Hashmi and JANAM (6 lectures) Theatre after Globalization : social theories of globalization (Arjun Ap padurai et al.), theatre after globalization, multicultural theatre, Indian English theatre, select playtext (Mahesh Dattani’s Bravely Fought the Queen/Asif Currimbhoy’s Goa) (5 lectures) Textbooks 1. 1. Lal, A., (ed.) (2009), Theatres of India: A Concise Companion, Oxford University Press. 2. 2. Dharwadker, A., (2005), Theatres of Independence: Drama, Theory and Urban Performance in India since 1947, University of Iowa Press. 3. 3. Bhatia, N., (ed.) (2009), Modern Indian Theatre: A Reader, Oxford University Press. 4. Damodaran, S., (2017), The Radical Impulse: Music in the Tradition of the Indian People’s Theatre Association, Tulika. 5. 4. Bharucha, R., (1983), Rehearsals of Revolution: The Political Theater of Bengal , University of Hawaii Press. 6. 5. Bharucha, R., (2001), The Politics of Cultural Practice: Thinking through Theatre in an Age of Globalization, Oxford University Press. 7. 6. Malini Bhattacharya’s IPTA articles in Journal of Arts and Ideas, Sangeet Natak, Anita Cherian’s article on Sangeet Natak Akademi reports in Third Frame will be provided by the instructor. 8. Translated/original playtexts and writings of Rakesh, Sircar, Karnad, Tendulkar, Elkunchwar, Alekar, Kambar, Swaminathan, Kanhailal, Panikkar, Tanvir, Dattani, Currimbhoy, Dutt as published

92 Title Asian American Literature Number HSL7XXX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0[3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives: The Instructor will: 4. 1. Introduce students to the literary field of Asian American literature. 5. 2. Look into three kinds of prose narratives, namely, immigration narratives, narratives of second- generation identity construction, and narratives emphasizing global or postcolonial perspectives. 6. 3. Demonstrate the dynamic relationship between Asian American literature and the histories of Asians in the US. 7. 4. Provide insights into settlement histories of the ethnic communities, legal discourses of immigration, multiracial hierarchy, multiculturalism, and neocolonialism in the US. Learning Outcomes: The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Understand how the standard racial categorization of Asian Americans belies their vastly different languages, histories and traditions in the US. 2. Identify the challenges that Asian Americans encou nter while undergoing the transition from “Asian” to “Asian American.” 3. Explore how Asian American literature can function as a political and racial agency in critiquing America-centrism and racial inequality in the US. Contents: Introducing the genre: Emergence of the category “Asian American”, Arrival of early immigrants specifically from East Asia (China, Korea, and Japan) and the Philippines, The later addition of groups from Southeast Asia, South Asia, and West Asia, Asian Americans disowning immigr ants from other parts of Asia, Immigration policy of the US, Exclusion and deportation, Naturalization of Asians. (7 lectures) Close Textual Readings and Conversations : Maxine Hong Kingston (5 Lectures), Amy Tan (5 Lectures), Bharati Mukherjee (5 Lectures) , Jhumpa Lahiri (5 Lectures), John Okada (5 Lectures), Chang-Rae Lee (5 Lectures), Le Thi Diem Thuy (5 Lectures) Textbooks 1. Maxine Hong Kingston’s The Woman Warrior 2. Amy Tan’s The Joy Luck Club/ The Kitchen God’s Wife/ The Hundred Secret Senses 3. Bharati Mukherjee’s Jasmine/ Wife/ The Middleman and Other Stories/ Holder of the World 4. Jhumpa Lahiri’s The Namesake/ Unaccustomed Earth/ Interpreter of Maladies 5. John Okada’s No-No Boy 6. Chang-Rae Lee’s Native Speaker 7. Le Thi Diem Thuy’s The Gangster We Are All Looking For Reference Books 1. Agnew, Vijay. Diaspora, Memory and Identity: A Search for Home, University of Toronto Press, 2005. 2. Bhabha, Homi K. Nation and Narration. Routledge, 1990. 3. Bhabha, Homi K. The Location of Culture. Routledge, 1994. 4. Brah, Avtar. Cartographies of Diaspora: Contested Identities. Routledge, 1996. 5. Braziel, Jana E, and Anita Mannur. (Eds.) Theorizing Diaspora. Blackwell, 2003. 6. Chan, J. P., et al. editors. The Big aiiieeeee! An Anthology of Chinese American and Japanese American Literature. Meridan, 1991. 7. Cheung, King-kok. (Ed.) An Interethnic Companion to Asian American Literature , Cambridge University Press, 1997. 7. Clifford, James. Routes: Travel and Translation in the Late Twentieth Century. Harvard UP, 1997. 8. Cohen, Robin and Carolin Fischer. (Eds.) Routledge Handbook of Diaspora Studies . Routledge, 2019.

94 Title World Literature and Global Cinema Number HSL7XX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The instructor will: 1. Help students to explore the intricacies of concepts such as world literature/ weltliteratur, national, transnational and/or global within the disciplines of literary and cinema studies 2. Help students to become familiar with some of the most significant phenomena in the history of post-globalization cinema 3. Make students familiar with the emergent categories such as slow cinema and discuss their efficacy as global concepts Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Map the trajectory from the national to the transnational conceptually, culturally and politically 2. Explore the methodological paradigm shift that the rise of transnationalism entails in various humanities disciplines 3. Develop acquaintance with contemporary research on transnationalism and cinema and consider the possibility of using transnationalism as a research method Contents Introducing world literature : Weltliteratur, the term borrowed from Goethe, the Franco Moretti intervention, literary mapping (10 lectures) World Literature and Its Complexities : Contemporary comparative literature dealing with the concept, works of Emily Apter and Pascale Casanova, world history of literature (10 lectures) Cinema and the Transnational: National cinema, the nation -state paradigm and its limitations, world cinema/transnational cinema and the interchangeability, the transnational waves (10 lectures) Contemporary Categ ories: Transnational as method, slow cinema and its discontents, correspondences/filmed letters of contemporary filmmakers (12 lectures) Textbooks 1. Casanova, P., (2004), The World Republic of Letters, Harvard University Press. 2. Goodwin, J., and Holbo, J., (eds.) (2011), Reading Graphs, Maps, Trees: Responses to Franco Moretti, Parlor Press. 3. Vitali, V., and Willemen, P., (eds.) (2006), Theorising National Cinema , British Film Institute. 4. Nagib, L., Perriam, C., and Dudrah, R., (eds.) (2006), Theorizing World Cinema, I. B. Tauris. 5. Ezra, E., and Rowden, T., (eds.) (2005), Transnational Cinema: The Film Reader , Routledge. Reference Book Luca, T. D., and Jorge, N. B., (eds.) (2016), Slow Cinema, Edinburgh University Press. 95 Title Globalization and Culture Number HSL4xx Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The Instructor will: 1. Introduce students to varied definitions of globalization including its nature, dynamics and consequences as well as its multiple expressions in various periods in history. 2. Examine the cultural dimensions of globalization through global institutions, global flows, and the circulation of commodities, ideas and practices. 3. Explore the rise of religious, social, nationalist and populist movements across the world that challenge/supplement globalization. Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Understand globalization as a historical and cultural phenomenon. 2. Apply theories and concepts in the study of globalization towards the understanding of specific cultural forms and their implications for economic and scientific development. 3. Critically engage with the proponents and dissidents of globalization and how they relate to our contemporary times. Contents When was Globalization: Globalization in History, Defining Globalization, Global-Local distinctions Globalization and Culture: Neoliberalism, Cultural homogenization, Rise of common cosmopolitan cultures, McDonaldization Global Flows: Circulation of cultural forms, commodities and practices (music, fashion, gaming, language, tourism and popular culture, innovation, scientific collaboration etc.) Globalization and its Discontents: The rise of populism, consumer citizenship, local and slow food movements, Anti-globalization movements Textbooks 1. Steger, M., (2017). Globalization: A very short introduction, Oxford University Press. 2. Barber, B., (1995). Jihad versus Mcworld, Times Books. 3. Stearns, P., Globalization in World History, Routledge. Reference Books 1. Diamond, J., (1997), Guns, Germs and Steel: The Fates of Human Societies, RHUK. 2. Appadurai, A., (1996), Modernity at Large: Cultural Dimensions of Globalization, 4th Edition, University of Minnesota Press. 3. Stiglitz, J., (2002), Globalization and its Discontents. W. W. Norton and Company. Online Course Material 1. SUNY Levin Institute, Globalization 101, http://www.globalization101.org/ 2. Roy, A. G., Globalization and Culture, NPTEL Course Material, Department of Humanities and Social Sciences, Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, https://nptel.ac.in/courses/109/105/109105113/#

96 Title Sociology of Science and Technology Number HSL7XX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. To help students conceptualize science and technology as embedded in culture, politics and sociality and understand how technical knowledge is produced in society. 2. To help students explore the dynamic relationship between technology and society and discover how technology and society influence each other. 3. To make students conversant with important and new concepts in science and technology studies in social anthropology. Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Comprehend technological progress as a social process 2. Find connections between science, technology and culture and think beyond simple binaries like ‘natural’ and ‘social’ sciences and ‘nature’ and ‘culture’. 3. Develop sensitivity towards an inclusive, sustainable use of technology and appreciate the significance of diversity in science studies Contents Introduction to the Sociology of Science – Introduction to the subject, its founding concepts and traditions, methods of doing STS studies, History of Science and its philosophical traditions – logical positivism, falsification and its critique (6 lectures) Methodology of Science and its social connections - Structure of scientific revolutions, Ethics and ethos in science and deviance in practice of science, the Matthew Effect, and practicing ‘agnostic’ science, scientific inventions as cultural capital, social life of scientists. (10 lectures) Social Construction of Science - Methods of representation in science, Ethnography of a laboratory, social construction of ‘realities’, social construction of na ture, Effect of social understanding of race and gender on production of scientific knowledge (10 lectures) STS as Social Science – Actor Network theory, Pasteurization and the world of non-humans, influence of science studies on social sciences, ecological understanding of the world, towards an inclusive understanding of the universe through STS. (10 lectures) Science and Technology in India - Science & Technology in Colonial India, Development of Indian Science, Science and Governance in India (6 lectures) Textbooks 1. Sismondo, S. (2010), An Introduction to Science and Technology Studies , 2nd Edition, Wiley Blackwell 2. Miller, D. et. al. edited (2012), Digital Anthropology, Berg. Reference Book 1. Felt U., Fouche, R. et. al. edited (2017), The Handbook of Science and Technology Studies , MIT Press Online Course Material 1. Mallick, S. Science, Technology and Society, NPTEL Course Material, Department of HSS, IIT Guwahati, https://onlinecourses.nptel.ac.in/noc17_hs26/preview 2. Mishra, A. Sociology of Science, NPTEL Course Material, Department of HSS, Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, https://onlinecourses.nptel.ac.in/noc18_hs09/preview

97 Title Culture, Art and Heritage Course No. HS 321 Department HSS L-T-P[C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Pre-requisite None Objectives: The Instructor will: 1. Make the course largely interdisciplinary in nature and draw on literature, history, heritage, film, cultural studies and technology in India and the world 2. Help the students in understanding the complex role of history and culture in the shaping of our societies and identities 3. Explore a large canvas of genres, from Indian mythology, cinema, theatre, protected monuments, historical movements, folk dance and heritage. Learning Outcomes: The student is expected to 1. be exposed to the diverse traditions of India and the world 2. develop an awareness and interest in indigenous traditions, heritage and technologies 3. d evelop an understanding to create national consciousness as objects of literary and cultural analysis Contents Culture: Introduction: The concept of Culture, Historicity and Definitions, Culture and The Nation, Uses of History in Contemporary India, Identity and Culture, Popular Culture, Visual Culture Heritage and Conservation: Built Heritage: Introduction, Structures and Conservation, Material and Architectures, Technology and Architecture, Restoration Architecture, Indian History and the role of Architecture and sculpture, Conservation and the role of Conservation Agencies, Natural Disasters and the role of Conservation. Intangible Heritage: Arts – Performing Arts (Music and Dance forms), Fine Arts (Painting), Literature centering around Myths, Legends and Epic Traditions, Oral Traditions, Traditional knowledge systems, Craftsmanship. Textbook Dalmia, V., and Sadana, R., (eds.) (2012), The Cambridge Companion to Modern Indian Culture , Cambridge University Press. Reference Book Kumar, K. J., (2000), Mass Communication in India, Jaico Publishing House. Online Course Material No specific material
