98 Course Title Gender and Society Course No. HSL7360 Department HSS Structure (L-T-P-C) 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Pre-requisite None Objectives 1. To provide conceptual, sociological tools and skillset for cr itiquing binary and ahistorical conceptions of gender 2. To offer critical understanding of gender in a globalized, transnational world 3. To offer critical understanding of gender representations in media, visual cultures, and technology Learning Outcomes 1. Critique binary and ahistorical conceptions of gender in society 2. Understand interrelatedness of local, global, and transnational contexts in shaping of gender Issues 3. Accept of shared responsibility for solving local and global experiences of gender inequality Contents Gender as social construction: Key concepts; Introductions; Historical and social constructions of gender (3 lectures); Gender in Colonial History (6 lectures) Gender across geo -social scales - Politics of the body; Marriage and the Family; Gender and the Nation; Gender and Migration (6 lectures) Feminisms - History and types of feminist movements; Transnational Feminisms (6 lectures) Gender, Science, and Technology - History of gender in science and technology; Household technologies; Medical technologies; Communication technologies; Video Games (7 lectures) Imagining and Representing Gender - Gender in Literatur e and Culture (3 lectures); Postcolonial Studies; Gender and “modernity” (4 lectures); Normativity, Subversions, and Queer Studies (4 lectures); Global Gender Politics (3 lectures) References 1. 99 Title Global Health Number HSL 7XXX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. To introduce basic concepts of global health, and its relevance globally, with special reference to lower and middle-income countries (LMICs). 2. To understand the various determinants of global health and policy options to address global public health issues. 3. To examine how medical technologies should be used to improve health in low and middle income countries. Learning Outcomes 1. 100 Title Health Policy, Systems, and Financing Number HSL7XXX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0[3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. Introduce critical and comparative understanding of the theory and practice of health policy with special focus on India. 2. Facilitate students to understand components of health systems and its financing mechanism. 3. Introduce different national level secondary health data sets and its relevance in research and policy making. Learning Outcomes 1. Realize the importance of health policy and how to define policy with special focus on India. 2. Have a brief overview of the evolution of Indians health policy since Independence. 3. Understand different components of health systems and its financing mechanism. 4. Identify available national level secondary datasets in the health sector and its relevance in research and policy making. Contents Making Health Policy: The health policy framework: context, process, and actors; power and policy process; the state and private sector in health policy; agenda setting; government and policy process; policy implementation and evaluation (10 lectures). Evolution of India’s Health Policy: Bhore Committee-1946; National Health Policy-1983, 2002, and 2017; Alma Atta Declaration -1978; National Rural Health Mission -2005; Ayushman Bharat Yojana-2018 (8 lectures). Understanding Health System: Service Delivery; health workforce; health information system; medical product; vaccines; and technology; Financing; leadership and governance (7 lectures). Healthcare financing: Health transition, diseases burden, and health expenditure pattern; collecting revenue, pooling risk, and purcha sing services; risk pooling mechanism; external assistance for health; improving health outcome (8 lectures). National Level Secondary Health Data Sets: National Sample Survey; National Family Health Survey; Census; Longitudinal Aging Study in India (8 lectures). Textbook 1. Buse, K., Mays, N., & Walt, G. (2012). Making health policy. McGraw-hill education (UK). 2. World Health Organization. (2007). Everybody's business -strengthening health systems to improve health outcomes: WHO's framework for action. 3. Gottret, P., & Schieber, G. (2006). Health financing revisited: a practitioner's guide. The World Bank. Reference Books/ Re 1. Blank, R., Burau, V., & Kuhlmann, E. (2017). Comparative health policy. Macmillan International Higher Education. 2. Mills, A., Bennett, S., & Russell, S. (2001). The challenge of health sector reform: What must governments do? New York: St. 3. Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India (2017). National Health Policy - 2017. New Delhi 4. Government of India (1946) ‘Report of the Health Survey and Development Committee (Bhore Committee) IV. Manager of Publications; Delhi. Online Course Materials Emanuel E.J. Economics of Healthcare Delivery. University of Pennsylvania: https://www.who.int/health_financing/training/e-learning-course-on-health-financing-policy-for- uhc/en/

101 Title History and Philosophy of Science Number HSL7410 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. To introduce philosophical origins and foundations of science 2. To provide a deeper insight into the evolution of science and scientific methodology 3. To help students identifying the relationship between science, philosophy, and society Learning Outcomes 1. Students will have a realistic and rational approach towards different conceptions of science 2. The course may make students capable to analyze manifold philosophical issues associated with recent advancement of sciences 3. The course will nurture the skill to think analytically and critically Contents Historical and Philosophical Foundations of Science : Reciprocal Relationship between Science and Philosophy; Search for the Truth: History of Philosophy, Science, and Philosophy of Science; Scientific Methodology; Possibility of Knowledge; Laws of Nature; Limits of the Tools; Human Reason and Experience; Historic Interpolation (8 lectures) Major Philosophic (and Scientific) Concepts : Explanation; Causation; Evidence; Prediction; Probability; Determinism; Reduction; Generalization; Universals; Space and Time; Modeling and Simulation; Truth Value (12 lectures) Major Debates: Availability of Objectivity and Possibility of Subjectivity; Truth Discovery and Truth Creation; Theory Choice; The Turn to the Best Explanation; Underdetermination of Theories by Evidence; Bayesianism; Empiricism; Essentialism; Explanati on; Realism and Antirealism; Structure of Scientific Revolutions; Nature of Scientific Explanations; Truth and/or Consensus; Historical Approach; The Pragmatic View (12 lectures) Central Issues in Life Sciences: Biological Laws and Theories of Causation; T eleology; Theory of Natural Selection; Leaps and Randomness; Complexity, Indeterminacy, and Directionality; Biological Reductionism and Determinism; Darwin and Darwinism; Genetic Interventions; Eugenics; Enhancement; Nature of Scientific Discourses (10 lec tures) Reference Books 1. Kuhn, T.S. (2012). The Structure of Scientific Revolutions , Chicago: University of Chicago Press. 2. Kuhn, T.S. (1992). The Copernican Revolution, Cambridge: Harvard University Press. 3. Salmon, M.H. et al. (1992). Introduction to the Philosophy of Science , New Jersey: Prentice-Hall. 4. Psillos, S. & Curd, M. (2008). The Routledge Companion to Philosophy of Science , London: Routledge. 5. Darwin, C. (1859). On the Origin of Species, London: Murray Press. 6. Rosenberg, A & McShea, D.W. (2008). Philosophy of Biology, London: Routledge. 7. Meijers, A. (2009). Philosophy of Technology and Engineering Sciences , Amsterdam: Elsevier. 8. Dawkins, R. (2006). The Selfish Gene, 30th edition, London: Oxford University Press. 9. Dawkins, R. (1996). The Blind Watchmaker, London: W.W. Norton. Online Course Material 1. Isaacs, I. Philosophy of Science, 2020, Online Course, Oxford University, https://www.conted.ox.ac.uk/courses/philosophy-of-science-online

102 Title Foundations of Sustainability Number HSL4040 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. To help students seriously considering responsible uses of science and technology 2. To motivate students to examine critically the potential uses of technological knowledge and artifacts 3. To provide acquaintance with normative commitments of an engineer/technologist Learning Outcomes 1. Students shall be competent to assess the idea of sustainability with regard to possible applications of technological skills 2. Intellectual skills of critical thinking, unbiased assessment, and constructive decision making shall be nurtured 3. Sensitivity towards global concern for a sustainable future shall be promoted Contents Technological and Ethical Rationality : Thinking Like an Engineer; Normativity of Science and Technology; Technological Imperatives and Social Imperatives; Sciences, Values, and Value of Sciences. (6 lectures) The Idea of Sustainability: Emergence and Scope of Sustainability Science; Basic Principles of Sustainable Development; Report to the Club of Rome; UN Report; Concern for the Future; Evolutionary Roots of Environmental Problems (8 lectures) Plausible Applications of Technologies and Sustainability Con cerns: Recent Advancements in Technologies; Impacts on Life Forms and Ecology; Methods for and Approaches to Evaluating Susceptibility of Ecological Systems to Hazardous Chemicals; Global Pollution and Health Risks (8 lectures) Technology, Risks, and Ethic s: Perception of Risk; Social Benefits versus Technological Risk; Justifying Risk; Moral Acceptability of Risk; Rise of Risk and Decline of Politics; Role of International Cooperation (8 lectures) Uncertainty, Assessment and Precautionary Principle : Precau tionary Principle; Future Technologies; Ethics, Technological Development, and Uncertainty; Ethics in Technological Culture; Pragmatic Turn (12 lectures) Reference Books 1. Curry, P. (2011). Ecological Ethics, Cambridge: Polity Press. 2. Attfield, R. (2003). Environmental Ethics. Cambridge: Polity Press 3. Deane-Drummond, C.E. (2004). The Ethics of Nature. Oxford: Blackwell. 4. Meadows, H.W. et al. (1972). The Limits to Growth. Washington: Potomac Associates. Online Resources 1. United Nations. Sustainable Development Goals, 2020, https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/ 2. United Nations. Sustainable Development Knowledge Platform, 2020, https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org

103 Title Climate Change and Society Number HS 7xx Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives: The Instructor will: 1. Introduce students to scientific technological, historical, social, economic, political, cultural and ethical aspects of climate change within India and globally. 2. Contextualize climate change in terms of global politics, technologies, policies, gender, aesthetics, activism, and the anthropocene. 3. Facilitate the student to understand trans -disciplinary trajectories and their role in t he complex interactions between climate, actors, scales, government, technology, civil society, cultural/social structures. Learning Outcomes: The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Critically analyze contemporary debates and perspectives on climate change histories, policies, technologies, alternative voices and human responses. 2. Engage in respectful discussions, think creatively and critically to provide meaningful solutions to climate related issues. 3. Reflect upon and acknowledge one’s moral and ethical obligations to the planet in the future. Contents Introduction to Climate Change (2 lectures) Global Genres and Positions Genres: Pastoral, Wilderness, Dwelling, Apocalypse (2 Lectures) Positions: Social Ecology, Spiritual Ecology, Scientific Conservation, Green Politics, Ecofeminism, Deep Ecology, Bioregionalism, Tinai, Chipko Movement (2 Lectures) Gender and environment: Is Climate Change gender neutral (research & perspectives), Climate change through the lens of intersectionality , climate change impact on gender in context of water, gender and food security, gender and land rights and, gender and health (6 lectures) Women Writing Nature: Rachel Carson, Terry Tempest Williams, Sunitha Narayan, Mahaswetha Devi and Ambai (5 lectures) Eco-Cinema: An Inconvenient Truth, Chasing the Ice, Paan, Godavari, Before the Flood, The Day After Tomorrow (5 lectures) Policy and Climate Change: Global and Indian perspectives and SDGs, climate smart agriculture, climate finance, climate change and co nflict/violence, climate change -induced migration (climate refugees) and displacement, adaptation to climate change, climate and environmental justice (8 lectures) Anthropocene or the Human Impact on Climate Change: Climate change and agriculture - a historical analysis in the Indian context, climate change and disasters, ocean and climate change (5 lectures) Anthropocene and Climate Change Narratives: Amitav Ghosh – Great Derangement, Vandana Shiva – Water Wars, Cli -fi – Amitav Ghosh (Gun Island), Barbara Kingsolver (Flight Behaviour), SunithaNarain – Conflicts of Interest, Elizabeth Kolbert -The Sixth Extinction: AnUnnatural History, Donna Haraway – Tentacular Thinking: Anthropocene, Capitolocene and Chthulucene (6 lectures) Text Book: A handbook with all the study material will be given to the students. The course will also include a field trip. Reference Books 1. Gadgil, M., and Guha, R., (1993), This Fissured Land: An Ecological History of India. UCLA. 2. Giddens, A., (2008), The Politics of Climate Change. Policy Network Paper. 3. Nixon, Rob., (2011), Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor. Harvard University Press. 4. Bidwai, Praful., (2012), The Politics of Climate Change and the Global Crisis: Mortgaging Our Future, Orient BlackSwan. 5. Garrard, G., (2012). Ecocriticism: The New Ecocritical Idiom. Routledge. 6. Guha, R., (2014), Environmentalism: A Global History. Penguin Books. 7. Kolbert, E., (2014), The Sixth Extinction: An Unnatural History. Bloomsbury. 8. Dunlap, R., and Brulle, R.J., (2015), Climate Change and Society: Sociological Perspectives, OUP.

105 Title Politics of Water Governance Number HSL7420 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The Instructor will: 1. Provide conceptual sociological critical understanding on water governance through global, national policies and geo -politics; and the multiple challenges faced by the societies to address water issues. 2. Introduce students/young engineers to examine technologies through the lens of sustainability question and understand how technologies impacts the environment, industries and local communities’ livelihood through the case of water. 3. Facilitate the students to understand trans-disciplinary pathways to explore conceptual and empirical questions concerning water scarcity, technologies, water pollution, uncertainty/rights and access to water resources, and the cultural politics of water development. Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Interpret the theories and concepts underlying multiple levels of water governance, and contemporary global water debates around SDGs from a local/regional perspective. 2. Reflect on the concepts of sustainability when developing technologies and analyze water nexus with livelihoods, technologies and pollution. 3. By the end of the course, students/young engineers will be able to understand the politics and the socio -economics of water pol lution and the sustainability question of the technologies and its relation with water. Contents Water management across space and time: historical narrative (4 lectures) Major paradigm shifts in water governance: groundwater governance; politics and soci o- economics of water pollution, political ecology of water (5 lectures) Water as wicked problem: water laws/regulations/policy in India, Water conflicts in India and South-Asia trans-boundary water conflicts (5 lectures) Gender and water: engineering masculinities in water governance (3 lectures) Water rights and water justice: global politics of water grabbing; new spaces for water justice (4 lectures) Social scientific understanding of socio-technical systems: politics of dams; virtual water flow, cost-benefit analysis of technologies and the livelihoods surrounding water (5 lectures) Foucauldian discourse analyses: new water standards and practices of multinational corporations (5 lectures) Water-climate change: water-food security nexus, water -agriculture nexus, water -energy nexus (5 lectures) Water centric SDGs: SDGs 2, 6, 14, India and UN (5 lectures) Textbook: A handbook with all the study material will be given to the students. The course will also include a field trip. Reference Books 1. Mehta, L., (2005), The Politics and Poetics of Water: The Naturalisation of Scarcity of Western India, Orient Longman. 2. Shah, T., (2009), Taming the Anarchy: Groundwater Governance in South Asia. Resource for Future, John Hopkins University Press. 3. Zwarteveen. M.Z., Ahmed, S. and Gautam, S.R., (2012), Diverting the flow: Gender equity and water in South Asia, Zubaan. 4. Sultana, F., and Loftus, A., (ed.) (2012), The Right to Water: Politics, Governance and Social Struggles, Routledge. 5. Lankford, B., Bakker, K., Zeitoun, M., and Conway, D., (eds.) (2013), Water Security Principles, Perspectives and Practices, 1st Edition. Routledge. 6. Naz, F. (2014), The Socio -cultural Context of Water: Study of a Gujarat Village , Orient Blackswan.

107 Title Aesthetics Number 32208 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. Analysis of key philosophical attempts which address issues related to beauty and art 2. Explication of theoretical aspects related to the judgment of taste 3. Evaluation of issues in aesthetics related to design. Learning Outcomes 1. Understand the nature and function of art with the help of theories in aesthetics 2. Understand the nature and function of beauty 3. Identify the role of aesthetics in design Contents The Nature of Beauty and Art : Plato and Aristotle: The Symposium, an analysis of beauty; Imitation and Inspiration: the common thread in all art forms; Aesthetic Independence: Aristotle’s Poetics (10 lectures) Kritik der Urteilskraft (Critique of Judgment ): Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Aesthetic Judgment: discussions on aesthetic experience and judgment; The ‘beautiful’: judgments on beauty and further interpretations. The ‘Sublime’: the power of reason over nature; ‘Pleasure’: intentionality in enjoyment (8 lectures) Existentialist Perspectives: Nietzsche, the ‘genius’ and creativity; Life: the ‘absurd’ and human freedom in expressions of art; Existentialism and Art: the purpose of art in a meaningless world; Existentialist art and the ‘audience’: spectator’s vantage point (8 lectures) Feminist perspectives in A esthetics: Feminism: a critique of traditional Western ideologies on art; The Body: in art, science and philosophy; Aesthetic Categories: the feminine lens; Aesthetics: in everyday life; Post- Modernism and Aesthetics; Post-Modern Art (8 lectures) Aesthetics of Design: The Methodology, Functionality and Aesthetics: the importance of design; Factors in Design: culture, scope and use; Case Studies: industrial culture and design of products (8 lectures) Reference Books 1. Aristotle. (1996) Poetics, Heath, Malcolm (Trans.), London: Penguin. 2. Forsey, Jane. (2013). The Aesthetics of Design, New York: Oxford University Press. 3. Gordon, Graham. (1997). Matthews, Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 5. Plato. (2001).Symposium, Benardete, Seth (Trans.), Chicago: The University of Chicago Press. 6. Sheppard, Anne. (1987). Aesthetics: An Introduction to t he Philosophy of Art, Oxford: Oxford University Press. 7. Davies, Stephen., Higgins, M. Kathleen., Hopkins, Robert ( et al ) (Eds). (2009). A Companion to Aesthetics, MA: Blackwell. Online Course Material 1. Grant, J. Aesthetics and Philosophy of Art, 2020, Online Course, Oxford University, https://podcasts.ox.ac.uk/series/aesthetics-and-philosophy-art-lectures

109 Title Consciousness Number HS729 Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The Instructor will: 1. Help the student appreciate the problem of consciousness 2. Help the student realise how different approaches to the study of consciousness arise out of different philosophical assumptions Learning Outcomes 1- Being able to understand how the problem of consciousness is significant in the overall task of explaining human cognitive capacity. 2- Being able to appreciate how insights from d ifferent approaches can be harnessed to build up an account of consciousness. Lecture Modules/Contents: The problem of Consciousness: Scientific and Philosophical Approaches to Consciousness Consciousness as a biological phenomenon: Need for unified research programme, multi level explanation. Explanation in the biological sciences. Major Theories of consciousness: Neural correlates, higher order thought theory, multiple drafts model, attention schema model. Illusionism about consciousness. Different Types of Consciousness: access consciousness and phenomenal consciousness, altered states of consciousness. Function of Consciousness: Consciousness as an epiphenomenon, global work space theory, panpsychism. Binding and phenomenal unity of consciousness: binding problem, cognitive mechanisms of phenomenal unity, neural mechanisms of binding. Evolution of consciousness, Self and Freewill. Reference Books: 1. Revonsuo A(2009) Inner Presence MIT Press. 2. Baars, B.J. (1997). In the Theater of Consciousness: The Workspace of the Mind . NY: Oxford University Press. 3. Metzinger, T. (Ed.) (1995). Conscious Experience. USA: Allen Press 4. Metzinger T(2009) The Ego Tunnell Basic Books

114 Title Consumer Culture and Commodities Number HS 7xx Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives: The Instructor will: 1. Facilitate students to understand and critically investigate consumption in contemporary, urban life. 2. Acquaint students with theories that will help them locate consumption vis -à-vis sociocultural contexts, identities, and markets. 3. Elaborate key areas of consumption such as shopping spaces and experiences, domesticity, advertising, tourism and fashion using examples from the Indian context. Learning Outcomes: The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Understand major concepts and theories in consumption and consumer culture. 2. Investigate processes of consumption empirically in various aspects of contemporary life. 3. Understand key political and moral concerns around consumption regarding ecology, sustainability, and socio-economic class. Contents Understanding Consumption: Theories of consumption, mass consumption, commodity culture, consumerism (Daniel Miller, Clifford Geertz, Fredric Jameson) Objects, Materials and Social Contexts: Theories of matter and materiality, thing theory, study of objects (Bill Brown, Mary Douglas, Arjun Appadurai, Jean Baudrillard, Tim Ingold) Media and Consumerism: Advertising, consu mption, liberalization, middle -class lifestyles, conspicuous consumption in the Indian context (William Mazzarella, Leela Fernandes, Osella and Osella, Ritty Lukose) Textbooks 1. Sassatelli, R., (2007), Consumer culture: History, theory and politics, Sage. 2. Miller, D., (1987), Material Culture and Mass Consumption. 1st Edition, Wiley-Blackwell. Reference Books 1. Douglas, M. and Isherwood,B., (1996), The World of Goods: Towards an Anthropology of Consumption, Routledge. 2. Corrigan, P., (1997), The Sociology of Consumption, Sage. 3. Appadurai, A., (1986), The Social Life of Things: Commodities in Cultural Perspective , 1 st Edition, Cambridge University Press. 4. Falk, P, and Campbell, C., (eds.). (1997), The Shopping Experience, Sage. Online Course Material 1. https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/consumer-culture 2. https://www.coursera.org/learn/market-power

115 Title Civilizations, Cultures, and Technologies Number DHL6XX0 Department IDRP: DH L-T-P [C] 3–0–0 [3] Offered for M.Sc. DH First Year only; B.Tech Electives; B.Tech Minor in DH Type Compulsory for DH and Elective for all others Prerequisite None Objectives 1. This course introduces students to important historical and sociocultural processes that have crafted technologies over time and across civilizations. 2. Recognize how technological developments are related to socio -cultural values and practices and understand the roots of current technological society(ies) Learning Outcomes 1. Students will be able to appreciate that technology is not an isolated, literate enterprise, it rather produces structures, machines, processes, systems that impact and inflect societies and civilizations Contents 1. What is Technology - History of Civilizations and role of technology (Classical and 2. Early Modern Philosophy); Narrative(s) of Progress; Industrial Revolution(s); Industry and Innovation; Culture of Invention 3. Revolution, Enlightenment and the Rise of Modern Science 4. Social Construction of Technology - Colonial Technology (Race, Gender, Sciences and Technology); 5. Communication, Transportation and the changing world 6. Diffusion of Technologies and transfer of technology globally 7. The Development of the Computer Industry; Rise of the Internet and Digital Society(ies) 8. Industrialization, Commodification and the Environment; Biotechnology 9. Future of Science and Technology in the society and their changing relationship Textbook 1. Pacey, Arnold. Technology in World Civilization, 4th ed. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2001. 2. Volti, Rudi, Society and Technological Change, 4th ed. New York: Worth Publishers, 2001 Self Learning Material 1. 116 Title Images, Imaginations, and Digital Cultures Number DHL6XX0 Department IDRP: DH L-T-P-D [C] 3–0–0-0 [3] Offered for M.Sc., M.Tech, B.Tech Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. To familiarise students with the process of seeing as a social construct to explore the ways we produce, identify, understand, and consume images by studying visual materials from different historical and cultural milieu 2. To introduce students to how photography and images across time and space change visual discourse and people’s lives 3. By contextualising everyday visual culture within larger social debates around power, politics, identity and resistance, this course aims to create a consciousness about the communicative power of visual images, and to equip students with interpretive tools for the evaluation of images. Learning Outcomes 1. Students will be able to develop a sociological imagination of visual cultures and its impact on society 2. Students will be able to assemble a multi -perspective analysis of a given sociocultural issue related to images against local, global, international, and intercultural background 3. Map historical photographic concepts to current digital references. Content 1. Visual Cultures and the Process of ‘Seeing’: Subject -Object debate; The Spectacles of Modernity; Power, Knowledge and the Gaze (Imaging the ‘Other’) [10 Lectures] 2. Images as Performative Space [8 Lectures] 3. Visual Culture and Resistance - Representations, Culture, Media, and Markets [6 Lectures] 4. Digital media and Global Image (Visual Culture of Everyday Life) [10 Lectures] 5. Netnography/ Digital ethnography [8 Lectures] References Books 1. Karlekar, Malavika., (2013), Visual Histories: Photography in the Popular Imagination, Oxford University Press 2. Chaudhary, Zahid R., (2012), Afterimage of Empire: Photography in Nineteenth - Century India, University of Minnesota Press 3. Benjamin, Walter. 1936 (2008). The Age of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction. London: Penguin. 4. Nakamura, Lisa. 2008. Digitizing Race: Visual Cultures of the Internet. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.

117 Title Fundamentals of Digital Humanities Number DHL7010 Department IDRP-DH L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for B.Tech. (Cr>=100); M.Sc. (Cr >=30); M.Tech. (Cr.>0); Ph.D. (Cr.>0) Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. Introduce and explore a broad spectrum of perspectives on the Digital Humanities 2. Develop familiarity with a range of Digital Humanities projects, as well as the ability to evaluate the tools and methods involved in creating and analysing those projects 3. Critical and reflexive use of digital tools, technologies, and spaces by understanding that all technologies are complex and socially situated, through which humans make meaning Learning Outcomes 1. Appreciate and critically discuss Digital Humanities projects in light of current methods and theoretical approaches to the field 2. Explain how Digital Humanities methods and practices are applied in different disciplines 3. Skillset to plan, develop, and evaluate a Digital Humanities research project Fractal Course Contents Fractal 1: Digital Humanities: Emerging Contours (DHL7011) Introduction: What is Digital Humanities, Evolution of classical disciplines into Digital Humanities Digital Cultural Heritage; Conceptualising DH projects; Interdisciplinary style of proposal writing [4 Lectures] Computational Humanities [3 Lectures] Digital Embodiment: Embodied Identities in Digital Society; Bias and Privilege – Marginalised Histories; Cyborgs, Gender, Space, and Place in Digital Societies [4 Lectures] Literature and Technology, Text Analysis, Data Visualisation [3 Lectures] Hands-on Exercises 1. Identifying DH projects from traditional projects: Concrete examples and a range of approaches to DH from the traditional disciplines. 2. Digital Humanities Project Critiques: Exploring the project goals, what type of data it used, how that data was found and/or transformed, what technologies were used, and why. References Books 1. Gere, C., (2008), Digital Culture, 2nd Edition, London: Reaktion Books Limited 2. Bentkowska-Kafel, A., Cashen, T., and Gardiner, H. (Eds.) (2009), Digital Visual Culture: Theory and Practice, Bristol and Chicago: Intellect Books 3. Karaganis, J. (Ed.), (2007), Structures of Participation in Digital Culture, Social Science Research Council, Columbia University Press Online-course material Digital Humanities Seminar Video Archive of the Open University, UK, http://www.open.ac.uk/arts/research/digital-humanities/videos Fractal 2: Data and Knowledge representations (DHL7012) Introduction: Data Sources, Transcribing (Multimedia data), Conversation, Discourse Analysis [7 lectures] Knowledge Engineering: Ontological engineering, Representation of Ontologies, Common Logic, RDFS, Web Ontology Language (OWL), Topic Maps, Multimedia Web Ontology La nguage, Applications [ 7 Lectures] Hands-on Exercises

Provide a critical understanding regarding the artistic, political and technical facets of the internet and other emergent media that will help students better understand the contemporary paradigms in the field of network studies. 3. Allow students to develop a self reflexive understanding and a critical approach to web-based and computational cultures, through exposure to divergent perspectives on data, governance and society especially in the historical, social, cultural and economic context of India. Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. To understand the broad field of network cultures as a strategic instrument to diagnose political and aesthetic implications of user-driven computer mediated communication. 2. Interpret the theories and concepts underlying the technical, economic, social aspects of the network, and put it in dialogue with its everyday manifestations 3. By the end of the course, students will develop the capacity to create rational frameworks for the varied contexts of internet mediated communication: including design, activism, art, philosophy, political theory, and urban studies Contents Historical background: Society, Modern Science, and Technology (4 lectures) Tracing a co ncise history of the development and teleology of network studies and network cultures by acknowledging relevant contributions from theorists including Aristotle, Kuhn, Fleck, Jassanof Hierarchies v/s Networks (4 lectures) Locating the complex dynamics, similarities and differences between hierarchies and networks through works of scholars from diverse disciplines and locations such as Niall Feguson, Tim Berners Lee, David Berry, Alexander Galloway, and Sandeep Mertia The Social, The Technological and its Overlaps (8 lectures) Situating the epistemic and ontological origins of networks in its social and technical contexts including the overlaps. Readings and case studies from Langdon Winner, Claude S. Fisher, David, J. Hess, Tarleton Gillespie, Alessandro Ludovico, Geert Lovink, and Gyan Prakash, Networks and Networlds (4 lectures) Differentiating between networks and networlds;Communication paradigms, the power frameworks and counter power potentialities that are espoused in such networks and networlds. Readings and Case studies from Castells, Apprich, Dragona, Lovink, Wüst. Brevini, Pasquale and Mbembe Algorithms, Big Data and Surveillance Capitalism in the Networked Age (8 lectures) Analyzing Big Data, Open Data Algorithmic biases and Surveillance Capitalism within network societies. Readings and case studies from Gitelman, Boyd, Zuboff, Beer, Manovich, Driscoll and Walker) The Gender of Networks (4 lectures) Understanding the linkages, interactions and procesess through which gendered bodie s and networks interact. Readings from Wajcman, Haraway, Cupples, and Bay Networks and New Becomings (6 lectures) Analyzing the anomalous objects and processes in digitally networked cultures and the new possibilities and challenges that they engender, especially in a post Covid 19 landscape. Readings and case studies from Parrika, Loes Bogers, Letizia Chiappini, Duncan J. Watts & Steven H. Strogatz , Stefania Milan, Emiliano Treré and Silvia Masiero, and The Alan Turing InstituteThe Analog lives of Networked Digital Data in India (4 lectures) Afterlives of data and computational cultures in the context of the Global South, with a specific focus on India. 123 Title Masculinities in/and the Global South Number HSL 7xx Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The Instructor will: 1. Introduce students to the societal structures and expectations through which the gendered individual emerges as an integrated physiological, psychological, and socio -political being 2. Locate how the postcolonial nation state and masculine behaviours intersect in the Global South through in-depth case studies and analysis of policy reports as well as cultural artifacts related to current environments, health, family, relationships, and aging 3. Critically examine masculine expectations and behaviors in contemporary society, with a specific focus on India Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. To understand the broad field of Masculinity Studies and the construction of masculinities in sports, family, work and other social relationships 2. Examine th e concepts underlying heteropatriarchal assumptions about masculinity and the various gendered experiences of the male body based in citizenship, caste, class, occupation, physical ability and sexuality 3. By the end of the course, students will develop the capacity to understand and develop rational frameworks for the varied contexts of hegemonic, hyper and hypo-masculinities in diverse social and professional contexts Contents The Phenomenology and Materiality of Bodies (6 lectures) : Introduction to power, essence, embodiment and volatility in relation to gendered bodies through the works of Merleau-Ponty, Foucault, Irigaray, Cixous, de Beauvoir, Fuss and Grosz Gender and Performativity (8 lectures): Locating through the works of Butler, Halberstam, Bordo and Douglas how gendered behaviour and sexual identity differ, intersect and create dissonances based within the specificities of our geographical and social positions Bodies, Spaces and Borders (6 lectures): Examine how gendered bodies are performed and determined within the determining variables of spatial contexts and bordered zones. Readings from Sara Ahmed, Mohanty, Hooper, De Certeau, Debord, Massey and Soja Men, manhood and masculinities (12 lectures): Tracing the historical and social construc tions of hegemonic, hypo and hypermasculinities in various local, regional and national contexts. Readings from Connell, Kimmel, Messerschimdt, Dasgupta, Gokulsingh, Kabesh, McRuer, Krishnaswamy, Sinha and Puar Mediations, Violence and Manhood (6 lectures) : Examining the intrinsic role of violence in the construction of dominant masculinities especially in postcolonial spaces and the role of the media in legitimizing such constructions of manhood. Readings and viewings from Klaus Thewleit, Jackson Katz, Eric Anderson, Sanjay Srivastava, Mike Donaldson, Jon Mckenzie and others Digital masculinities and its Discontents (4 lectures): Deciphering how digital spaces configure new forms of masculinities and its effects on both online and offline spaces. Readings from Roy, Currier, Garlick, Chowdhury and others. Textbook: A curated course artifact with all the study material will be given to the students. Additional Materials: 1. Fuss, Essentially Speaking 2. Grosz, Volatile Bodies 3. Hatty, Masculinities, Violence and Culture 4. Hooper, Manly State 5. Jarvis, The Male Body at War 6. Kimmel, Manhood in America 7. Lingis, Foreign Bodies 8. McKenzie, Perform or Else 9. Theweleit, Male Fantasies (Vol.2)

125 Title Energy Humanities Number HSL7XX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The Instructor will: 1. Help students in exploring the intricacies of Energy Humanities and the social, political, and historical contexts which engender this interdisciplinary field 2. Make students familiar with the many modes, forms and practices from the humanities, social sciences a nd natural sciences that constitute the ontological and methodological underpinnings of the Energy Humanities 3. Help students to become familiar with some of the most significant events and issues that frame the key debates in the Energy Humanities Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Critically read theoretical texts and public policy artifacts that are relevant to the framing of discourses of Energy Humanities 2. Understand associations between public institutions, national cultures, consumerism, and capitalist socio-politico-cultural dynamics that influence imaginaries of energy in contemporary culture 3. Develop acquaintance with contemporary scholarly writings on Energy Humanities Contents The Rise of Energy Humanities (8 lectures) The emergence of “Energy humanities” as a rapidly emerging field of scholarship that overcomes traditional boundaries between the humanities and natural sciences and between academic and applied research; highlighting the essential contributions, insights and methods that the humanities can make to areas of study and analysis that were once limited and siloed within the natural sciences Discourses around Energy Humanities (8 Lectures): Role of key sites of research on energy and culture—Comenius University in Bratislava (Slovakia), the Center for Energy and Environmental Research in the Human Sciences (CENHS) at Rice University and the Petrocultures Research Group at the University of Alberta —in developing discourses around Energy Humanities; social as well as environmental consequences of energy once it gets industrialized across the globe; exploring the history of energy use and energy transitions Energy and Modernity (12 lectures): The self -reflexive relationship between energy, rationality modernity, and capitalist ecologies of development; Role of critical theory in the humanities and social sciences to formulate an effective critique of the multiple narratives of Western centric enlightenment narrative of modernity and discussing the dive rse manifestations of this narrative within formulations of energy discourses; the progress and growth of Energy in the global North through colonialism and exploitation of the people and resources of the global South. A Critical Theory of Energy in the Anthropocene: (10 lectures) The ways in which energy humanities interrogates systems and processes promulgated by an energy -focused society; Petromyopia; the need to reenvision the theoretical lexicon and applied vocabularies of history, politics, philosophy, literary and cultural studies and the need to add energy as a key variable for imagining inquiry into humanistic questions in the Age of the Anthropocene; understanding the ontological positions of dominant and minority socio-political subjects who inhabit energy landscapes Energy Humanities and its Futures: (4 lectures): Locating the political and public discourse around key energy issues of the future and explore the role of energy within international relations; identify examples of best practices re garding climate change policy and how we can move toward solving our current energy and environmental dilemmas by making humanistic research a part of the conversation Textbooks A curated course artifact with all the study material will be given to the students Reference Books Nye, D. E. (1997). Electrifying America Social meanings of a new technology. MIT Press.

127 Course Title Theories of Intelligence Course No. CG4xx Department Science of Intelligence Structure (L-T-P [C]) 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. The course will provide the introductory overview of the concept of Intelligence. 2. Acquainting the student to the historical significance, and practical implication. 3. Develop comprehensive understanding and scientific underpinning of concept of Intelligence. Learning Outcomes 1. Develop scientific understanding of concept, measurement and application of intelligence. 2. Acquire Psychological explanation of Intelligence and apply it to other similar concepts. Contents Historical development and concept of Intelligence: Origin of study of intelligence in Psychology; Defining Intelligence: Philosophical and Psychological; Language and intelligence; Biological, racial and cultural difference in Intelligence (8 Lectures) Theories of Intelligence: Psychometric theories; cognitive theories; cognitive-contextual theories; and biological theories. (10 Lecture) Intelligence and related concepts : Social Intelligence; Emotional Intelligence; System Intelligence, Personality and Intelligence, Emotion and Intelligence. (8 Lectures) Measurement of Intelligence : Psychometric assessment; Psychophysiological assessment (6 Lectures) Contemporary issues related to Intelligence: Intelligence and performance link, Human Intelligence in the era of artificial intelligence, Beyond Intelligence: concept of practical intelligence and concept of Wisdom (10 Lectures) Reference Book 1. 128 Course Title Advanced Cognitive Processes Course No. CG4xx Department Science of Intelligence L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. The course will provide the introductory overview of the Cognitive processes. 2. Understand fundamental cognitive theories of attention, memory, executive function and decision- making. 3. Develop comprehensive understanding and scientific underpinning of relation of brain, mind, and behavior. Learning Outcomes 1. Develop a knowledge base in cognitive Science and demonstrate familiarity with the major concepts, theoretical perspectives, empirical findings, and historical trends in cognitive Science. 2. Respect and use critical and creative thinking, skeptical inquiry, and the scientific approach to solve problems relating to mental processes. Contents Introduction: Introduction to cognitive Processes and Cognition, Foundation of Cognitive Psychology, the architecture of the Mind (4 Lectures) Knowledge and Mental Imagery: Concept formation, Different approach to Categorization, Semantic Network theory and model, Visual Imagery, Mental imagery, Cognitive Map, Schemas and Spatial cognition (5 Lecture) Metacognition and Memory: Basic process of memory encoding storage and retrieval, Short term memory/working memory, long term memory, Models of Memory, context and encoding specificity, metacognition and memory strategies, and forgetting, Memory for action, (5 Lectures) Language : Language acquisition, Language Comprehension, Speech perception, Constituent structure, Language Production and reading, Codes switching and Second Language Proficiency, Multilingualism (8 Lecture) Problem Solving and Creativity: : Classification of problems; Newell and simon’s Theory; Problem- solving Approaches, Nature and Measurement; Approaches to creativity, Factors affecting Creativity, Science of creative intelligence (7 Lectures) Reasoning and Decision making: Logical Reasoning and Decision Making, Theories of Thought processes; Decision making; Algorithms and Heuristics - representativeness, availability, anchoring and adjustment; Cognitive biases in decision making. (8 Lectures) Cognition and Emotion : Quantifying Cogni tion and affect, Affect cognition relations in specific cognitive processes like perception, attention, memory and judgement, System Theory, Emotion regulation (5 Lectures) Reference Book 3. (8 Lectures) Cognition and Emotion : Quantifying Cogni tion and affect, Affect cognition relations in specific cognitive processes like perception, attention, memory and judgement, System Theory, Emotion regulation (5 Lectures) Reference Book 3. 129 Course Title Engineering Psychology Course No. HS 4XX Department HSS Structure (L-T-P [C]) 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The Instructor will: 1. The course will provide the introductory overview of the Human factor and Engineering Psychology. 2. This course will allow the students to recognize the integrated (systems) nature of Engineering Psychology, the centrality of human beings in systems design, and to use the topics covered and the available knowledge base to adapt the environment to people. . Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Identify human performance capacities and limitations in modern human-machine systems; 2. Develop a knowledge base in engineering Psychology and demonstrate familiarity with the major concepts, theoretical perspectives, empirical findings, and historical trends. 3. 130 Course Title Cognitive Psychology Course No. HS 7XX Department HSS Structure (L-T-P [C]) 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The Instructor will: 1. To learn the different ways of conceptualizing the concept of Cognitive Psychology and cognition. 2. To understand the cognitive processes Underlying Human Behavior. 3. Since there is no universal approach to study all “Cognition”, the present course will use a number of older and newer approaches for studying Cognition. Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. This course will provide tools that are needed to think critically about problems relating to cognition and Human Behavior. 2. The knowledge from the course will be useful in tackling everyday problems and attaining optimal solutions. 3. Knowledge about human cognitive systems can be used in designing sophisticated Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems that learn from mistakes and make our lives a lot easier to live. Contents Module 1: History, The cognitive Revolution, Philosophical issues, Theory and research in Human Cognition Module 2: Object Perception and Recognition, Attention, Review of different approaches, automaticity , consciousness, awareness Module 3: Human and Artificial Intelligence, memory, visual and spatial memory, memory of general knowledge, concept formation Module 4: Language skills, thought process , Problem solving and creativity, Reasoning and decision making Reference Book 1. Galotti, K. M. (2017). Cognitive psychology in and out of the laboratory. Sage Publications. 2. P. Thagard, (2005), Mind: Introduction to Cognitive Science, 2nd Edition. MIT Press. 3. Sternberg, R. J., Sternberg, K.,(2012). Cognitive psychology. Cengage Learning Press. Supplementary Readings: Research article related to recent trends in Cognitive Psychology research Online Resource 1. Professor Michela Massimi et. al., Philosophy and the Sciences: Introduction to the Philosophy of Cognitive Sciences, coursera. https://www.coursera.org/learn/philosophy-cognitive- sciences 2. Professor Barbara Oakley et. al., Learning How to Learn: Powerful mental tools to help you master tough subjects, Coursera. https://www.coursera.org/learn/learning-how-to-learn 3. Professor Steve Joordens, Introduction to Psychology, Coursera, https://www.coursera.org/learn/introduction-psych

131 Course Title Introduction to Cognitive Neuroscience Course No. HS 7XX Department HSS L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for UG and PhD Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives The Instructor will: 1. To learn about the fundamentals of Neuroscience. 2. To understand the role of brain imaging in Neuroscience. Learning Outcomes The students are expected to have the ability to: 1. Demonstrate familiarity with basic anatomy and physiology of the Brain. 2. Explain how the brain allows us to do every day behaviour. 3. Understand the neuroanatomy, different functional aspect of brain and principles of signal processing in Brain. Contents Module 1: Introduction to cognitive Neuroscience, Neuroanatomy, Neuron, Action Potential, Sensory processing and motor systems Module 2: Behavioural measure of Cognition, Neuroimaging Methods in Cognitive Neuroscience, EEG, fMRI Module 3: Neural process of Attention, Vision, Language, motor control, Navigation, and Memory, Module 4: LTP and Synapses, Value based decision making, Reinf orcement Learning, Emotion and Social Cognition, Potential societal implication of Cognitive Neuroscience Reference Book 1. 132 sssCourse Title Introduction to Cultural Studies Course No. DHL7XX0 Department IDRP-DH Structure (L-T-P-D [C]) 3-0-0-0 [3] Offered for Ph.D. (Cr>=0); M.Sc. (Cr >=30); M.Tech. (Cr>=0); B.Tech. (Cr>=100) Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. Teach cultural studies as an interdisciplinary field which draws from and contributes to literature, media studies, cultural anthropology, and sociology amongst other disciplines. 2. Equip students with methods and frameworks to look at the central preoccupations of the field – identity, power, economy, culture, aesthetics, and social institutions. 3. Critically interrogate the benefits of cultural studies for both inter- and intra-disciplinary work. Learning Outcomes 1. Understand major theories relating to historical and emergent ideas of culture and social thought. 2. Investigate processes of cultural production, consumption, and preservation using conceptual tools from the field of cultural studies. 3. Contextualize the role, applications, and significance of culture in the digital age. Contents Culture in the 19th and 20th centuries: The Emergence of the Culture Concept, Evolution of Culture, Culture and the Industrial Revolution (5 lectures), The Culture Industry (Value and Meaning), Culture as Commodity (Mass Culture) (5 lectures) Culture and Politics: Aesthetics and Politics, National Culture, Cultural Semiotics and Political Life (5 lectures) Cultural Economy, Political Society (5 lectures) Culture and Pedagogy: Culture and the Disciplines - Literary Studies, Anthropology, Sociology, History, Linguistics/Philology, Visuality Studies, Political Science (6 lectures), Understanding the Two Cultures - Natural and Human Sciences, Addressing the Pedagogical and Intellectual Divide (5 lectures) Culture and Contemporary Life: Mapping the City, Urban Lives and Cultures (5 lectures), Knowledge Society, Technology, Precarity, Virtuality, Representation and Alternate Realities, Culture and Big Data (6 lectures) Text Books 1. Simon During. 1993. The Cultural Studies Reader. London: Routledge. 2. Toby Miller. 2001. A Companion to Cultural Studies. Malden: Blackwell. 3. Tom Boellstorff. 2015. Coming of Age in Second Life. Princeton: Princeton University Press. 4. Tejaswini Niranjana and Wang Xiaoming (eds.) 2015. Genealogies of the Asian Present: Situating Inter-Asia Cultural Studies. New Delhi: Orient Blackswan. 5. Andrew Milner. 1994. Contemporary Cultural Theory: An Introduction. London: University College London Press: London. Self Learning Material 1. Avishek Parui. 133 Course Title Analysis of Social Media Networks Course No. DHL7XX0 Department IDRP-DH L-T-P [C] 3-0-0 [3] Offered for Ph.D. (Cr>=0); M.Sc. (Cr >=30); M.Tech. (Cr>=0); B.Tech. (Cr>=100) Type Elective Prerequisite None Anti-requisite Social Networks, Social Network Analysis Objectives 1. The course introduces social network analysis, its mathematical foundations, and analyzing tools (Pajek or NodeXL or UCINET or Others). 2. Students will be introduced to different types of online networks and how to use them to answer social, economic, and other queries. Learning Outcomes 1. Students will be able to acquire social media data, formulate a hypothesis, and find an answer out of network data. Contents Introduction: Overview and Aspects of Networks, Ego Network, Characteristics of Social Networks. (3 Lectures) Mathematical Foundation for Social Network Analysis : Graphs, Matrices. (4 Lectures) Network Data: Sources, Sampling and bounding, Ethical considerations, and Collection Techniques. (4 Lectures) Network Data Management: Data format, Import, Cleaning, Transformation, Export, Visualization (3 Lectures) Information Diffusion Analysis: Centrality and Network Value, Influence, Epidemics Modeling (3 Lectures) Clustering and Grouping: Community detection, election campaign analysis. (3 Lectures) Networks in Their Surrounding Contexts : Homophily, Affiliation, Behaviour Modeling (3 Lectures) Markets and Strategic Interaction in Networks : Network Models of Markets, Bargaining and Power in Networks, Sponsored Search Markets, Network Effects and Economy (5 Lectures) Voting: Group Decision-Making, Information Aggregation (3 Lectures) Case Studies: Wiki Networks, YouTube, Flickr, Twitter, Facebook, Email Communication Network, Thread Network (11 Lectures) Text Books 1. David Easley and Jon Kleinberg (2013), Networks, Crowds, and Markets: Reasoning About a Highly Connected World, Cambridge University Press. 2. S. Borgatti, M. Everett and J.C. Johnson (2013), Analyzing Social Networks, Sage. 3. Derek L. Hansen, Ben Shneiderman and Marc A (2011), Analyzing Social Media Networks with NodeXL, Morgan Kaufmann Reference Books 1. Albert-Laszlo Barabasi (2016), Network Science, Cambridge University Press. 2. Mark Newman (2018), Networks, Oxford University Press 3. 134 Course Title Digital Storytelling Course No. DHL7XX0 Department IDRP-DH Structure (L -T-P- D [C]) 3-0-0-0 [3] Offered for Ph.D. (Cr>=0); M.Sc. (Cr >=30); M.Tech. (Cr>=0); B.Tech. (Cr>=100) Type Elective Prerequisite None Objectives 1. Understand and examine the new tenets of storytelling in the digital age through thoughtful analysis of trends, topics, consumption and digital tools used. 2. Analyze the changing roles of storytellers for news, businesses and nonprofit organizations. 3. Increase ability to come up with big, original ideas and creatively. Learning Outcomes 1. Develop a deeper sense of why and how we create and value stories 2. Learn about the ways digital communication technologies can expand and enhance narrative techniques 3. Develop narrative technique and the ways digital elements can interact with traditional written narratives to change the ways an audience experiences story 4. Learn how to match narrative techniques to an audience Contents New Technologies, Creative Opportunities : Evolution, Digital Entertainment, Convergence (4 Lectures) Creating Story-Rich Projects: Interactivity, Character Dialogue, Emotion (6 lectures), Social Media, Transmedia, Project creation (6 lectures) Harnessing Digital Storytelling for Pragmatic Goals: Teaching, Advertising, Training (9 Lectures) Media and Models: Mobile Device and Applications, Video Games (6 lectures), Interactive Cinema, Interactive TV, Electronic Kiosks, Immersive Environments (6 lectures) Digital Storytelling Tools (5 Lectures) Text Book 1. Joe Lambert (2013), Digital storytelling capturing lives, creating community, Routledge Publishers.

3 Title Systems Engineering and Project Management Number OAL7XX0 Department L-T-P [C] 1-0-0 [1] Offered for M.Tech Program Type Compulsory NGU Prerequisite Objectives Systems Engineering is an interdisciplinary approach and means to enable realization of successful systems. It focuses on defining requirements and then proceeding with design synthesis and system validation while considering the complete problem includin g operations, performance, test, manufacturing, cost, and schedule. This course intends to help students to develop the capability of systems thinking by introducing basics of systems engineering theory, methods, and tools through lecture and practice. Learning Outcomes After taking this class, you should be able to:  Develop a systems engineering plan for a realistic project.  Judge the applicability of any proposed process, strategy, or methodology for systems engineering  Apply systems engineering tools (e.g., requirements development and management, robust design, Design Structure Matrix) to realistic problems.  Know how to proactively design for and manage system lifecycle targets.  Understanding TRL and MRL concepts  Use project management tools Contents  Introduction - Terminology, Systems Thinking, Today’s Challenges (1 L)  Requirements Elicitation, Documenting System Requirements - Proper Specification Language, Depth of Definition (1 L)  Requirements Analysis - Context Diagrams, Functional Analysis, State Diagrams (2 L)  Requirements Validation - User Feedback Techniques, Requirements Reviews (1 L)  System Architecture - Subsystem Definition, Hierarchical Analysis, Design for Reuse, Interface Management (2 L)  Specialty Engineering - Producibility/Manufacturability, Reliability/Availability, Maintainability/Serviceability, Usability/User Interface, Design-to-Cost (2 L)  Managing Systems Engineering - Estimating, Planning, Tracking, System Engineering

Illustrate the significance of IPR in the context of Innovations and Demonstrate how information in IP data bases are used to enhance quality of innovations. 3. ACADEMIC PROGRAMMES Rules & Regulations ( ​ For Students enrolled from July 2019 onwards ​ ) Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur 1

1. ​ ​ INTRODUCTION Academic programmes at Indian Institute of Technology, Jodhpur are designed to develop the highest calibre human resource capable of understanding the new patterns of knowledge creation across disciplines obliterating traditional boundaries between science, humanities, social sciences and engineering. IIT Jodhpur aims to produce quality professionals who would be able to address profound and wide-ranging societal challenges of the 21st century such as energy, food, water, housing, mobility, and health. In addition to imparting scientific knowledge, IIT Jodhpur endeavours to inculcate human qualities of courage, integrity, fairness, humility and team effort among its graduates through curricular, co-curricular and extra-curricular activities on campus. The undergraduate academic programmes focus on developing a temper for the life long process of learning, creative thinking and exploring. The postgraduate academic programmes focus on developing a deep understanding of the subject of study coupled with creative inquisitiveness and the ability to address and solve new problems with a free and objective mind. The academic programmes are based on three tenets of (1) semester system, (2) Credit System and (3) Relative Grading. These academic programmes are administered by a duly constituted Academic Committee (AC) through the office of Academics. The AC will be chaired by Dean (Academics). In the absence of Dean (Academics), Associate Dean (Academics- PG)/Associate Dean (Academics- UG) will discharge the responsibilities of Dean (Academics). The Senate of the Institute has formulated a set of guidelines and rules to ensure a high standard of performance as well as for smooth functioning of the academic programmes. Within this broad set of guidelines, subject to the approval of Senate, different programmes can include additional academic requirements as deemed necessary for that programme. These academic programmes are continuously monitored by the Senate and make appropriate modifications/ improvements as and when necessary. 2. ACADEMIC SESSION The academic session normally runs from the end of July in one year to the middle of July in the next year. The academic session is divided into three parts: two regular semesters and a summer term as per the following timelines: Semester I: From the fourth week of July to the last week of November Semester II: From the last week of December to the last week of April Summer Term: From the middle of May to the middle of July. Excluding the days of the examinations, the total number of days of instruction in a semester is at least 70. 2.1 Academic Calendar The academic calendar gives the exact dates of all important events during the Academic Session, such as orientation, registration, the commencement of classes, adding and dropping of courses, submission of documents, examinations, submission of grades, project evaluation, declaration of results, mid-semester recess, and vacation. This calendar is approved by the Senate. 2

3. REGISTRATION a. Registration: ​ Students are required to register for prescribed credits as per the programme, on the dates specified in the Academic Calendar. If the student does not register by the date of registration, she/he can register by paying the fine and register before the date of late registration. b. Provisional Registration: ​ A fresh student joining the Institute, who is awaiting the final results of the qualifying examination, is allowed to register provisionally on submission of a certificate from her/his last Institute stating that she/he has appeared in the final examination of the qualifying degree. The student is required to submit documents of having passed the qualifying examination by the last date given in the Academic Calendar for the registration to be regularized. c. Late Registration: ​ If the student does not register by the date of late registration as mentioned in the Academic Calendar, he/she will be deregistered. The appeal against deregistration may be made to Chairman, Senate through Dean Academics. Chairman Senate may permit the continuation of registration on payment of an appropriate fine. d. Adding and Dropping of Courses: A student may add or drop course(s) with approval of the Faculty advisor till the last date of registration. e. Withdrawing from a Course: After the last date of add-drop, a student will have the option of withdrawing from a course. The last date of course withdrawal will be typically within four weeks from the beginning of the Semester as specified in the academic calendar. The withdrawn course will be mentioned in the Student’s grade card with a letter grade ‘W’. f. Cancellation of Semester Registration: Absence for a period of four or more weeks during a semester shall result in automatic cancellation of the registration of a student from all the courses in that semester. g. Summer course registration: ​ A department may offer summer courses to enable the students to clear their backlog courses and/or regular credit courses. A course will run during summer provided a faculty member(s) is available for running the course. The course is offered on approval of the Dean. 4. TEACHING AND EVALUATION 4.1 Teaching 4.1.1 ​ Medium of Instruction The medium of instruction is English. 4.1.2 Course Structure All courses have associated credits. Credits of a course are based on the number of contact hours for lectures, tutorials, and practicals A student on successful completion of the course with a passing grade will earn an equivalent number of credits. Based on the required academic maturity level of students for attending a course, a course is assigned a level. A course can consist of independent components which can be completed independently. These components are called fractals. A course is identified by a unique number. Following tables define all parameters related to course numbering scheme. 3

Elective courses of 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, or 600, level will run if a minimum of 10 students registers for the course. The main features of a self-study course are as follows: ● A student may be allowed to register for an elective course as a self-study course provided that the course is not running in that semester as a regular course or a student is not on campus during the course with prior approval of the competent authority. ● A student may also be permitted to register for a core or program compulsory course in self-study mode provided he/she has failed in it earlier and the course is not being offered as a regular course during that semester or a student is not on campus during the course with prior approval of the competent authority. ● Students should apply for a self-study course with the appropriate recommendation of a Course Coordinator and DUGC/DRC/IRC. The final sanction of a self-study course to a student is made by the Dean (Academics). ● Formal classroom engagement may not be there for a self-study course but laboratory, design and computation exercises will be conducted if they form an integral part of the course. ● The Course Coordinator conducts the assessment as per the evaluation norms for the award of letter grade at the end of the semester. ● A self-study course will appear with the approved course title on the transcript. ● Not exceeding 10% of the total graded credit can be opted as a self-study course. c) Independent Study Course Independent study enables a student to pursue course credit on an academic topic of interest under the supervision of a faculty member. The term independent does not mean not involving an Instructor but independent of regular class engagement. Self-disciplined and having a sense of own direction and goals are fundamental requirements of an Independent Study course. A student having CGPA more than or equal to 6.0 can opt for Independent Study courses with the recommendation of Supervising Professor. The main features of an independent-study course are as follows: ● A student may be permitted to register for a topic of interest as an independent-study course not exceeding 3 credits in self-study mode at most once during the program. Such independent study course will be counted toward open elective requirements of the program and will appear with the title “Independent Study” on the transcript. ● Students should apply for an independent study course with the appropriate recommendation of a Course Coordinator and DUGC/DRC/IRC. The final sanction of an independent-study course to a student is made by the Dean (Academics). ● Normally, no formal lectures will be held for an Independent Study course but laboratory, design and computation exercises will be conducted if they form an integral part of the course. ● The course will be arranged, planned and managed by a supervising professor. A course approved by the senate of IIT Jodhpur can be conducted through either (i) direct contact (ii) synchronized remote contact (iii) guided study mode or combination of these. In direct contact mode, coordinator or instructor will have a face to face physical interaction with the students. Synchronized remote contact mode would require the faculty and/or the students to be concurrently connected to the classroom interaction via electronic conferencing involving both audio and video communication. However, there has to be direct interaction between faculty and students for limited hours (typically 25%) of the stipulated contact hours. In guided study mode, a faculty would guide a single or a group of students to take up the study of an approved course via self-learning and discussion-oriented contact sessions. This mode can be also adopted for enabling a student to take up study of a new course, not yet approved by the Senate, under the supervision of a faculty. All formal evaluation component applicable to courses being run through any one of the above-mentioned modes will be conducted under direct physical supervision of a faculty. All laboratory component of a course requiring the use of the specialized facility will be conducted through direct contact. 4.1.7 Teaching Assignments The instructors and tutors for all courses to be offered during the semester are allocated by the Head of the Department hosting the Program. When faculty members of other Departments are also required to participate in teaching a particular course, the allocation shall be done in consultation with the Head of that Department. 4.1.8 Auditing of Courses A student may audit a course in addition to the prescribed academic load requirement with the permission of Dean (Academics) on the recommendations of Instructor of the course being audited and the Faculty Advisor. Under this arrangement, the course will be listed in the Grade Card of the student. 4.1.9 Attendance Requirements A student should have full attendance in each course. Unless the student takes leave of absence for valid reasons, the student has to attend every lecture, tutorial, or lab session. The attendance records must be made available to the student after every lecture. Even if the student’s attendance falls below 75%, the student will be allowed to appear for the exams. Students not meeting the attendance criterion of 75% will be required to score at least C grade to pass a course. These students would be awarded F grade if their marks are lower than the cut-off for C grade in a course. 4.2 ​ ​ Evaluation The performance of students in a course is evaluated continuously, using their interaction in the classroom, and performances in examinations, the laboratory work (if any), and term-papers and projects. The performance of students in a course is evaluated through examinations and on a continuous basis. The Senate will decide from time to time on the system of tests and examinations in each subject in each semester. 7

● Minor 1, Minor 2 and Major examinations are mandatory components of the evaluation of a regular 14-week long lecture course. The minor examinations shall be of 60 minutes duration and the major examination of 120 minutes. Fractal courses (less than 3 credits) must have at least one examination. ● The total weightage of examination component (three examinations for a 14 week-long course) shall be between 40% to 60% of the total weightage of evaluation measure. ● Evaluation policy has to be known from the first day of the class. ● The continuous evaluation may include but not limited to interaction in the classroom, quizzes, assignments, tutorials, laboratory work, term papers and projects. 5. ​ ​ GRADING SYSTEM 5.1 Letter Grades At the end of the semester, a student is awarded a relative letter grade in each course by the Instructor offering the course considering the performance of the student during the semester with respect to those of the other students registered in the course. It is proposed that ten regular letter grades, namely A*, A, A-, B, B-, C, C-, D, E and F shall be awarded in each course. Each letter grade is associated with a numerical equivalent on a 10-point scale shown in Table 5.1. In addition, there are four special letter grades, namely, I, S, X and U, which stand for Incomplete, Satisfactory, Thesis Continuation and Unsatisfactory, respectively. The faculty member shall upload grade on the portal as per the stipulated time schedule. Table 5.1 ​ Letter grade and its equivalent grade points S.N. 2 E ‘E’ Grade will be awarded to a student who has scored marks less than the cutoff marks for ‘D’ Grade and has met the attendance criterion of the institute. Students who obtain an ‘E’ Grade will be eligible to appear in an additional examination. If they perform satisfactorily, they become eligible for getting the ‘E’ grade converted to a ‘D’ Grade, otherwise, they will continue to have ‘E’ Grade. The student will have only one chance to appear for the additional examination for an ‘E’ Grade. The additional examination will be conducted within the first week of the next semester. The date of additional examination of Institute core courses for undergraduate students centrally notified, while for all other courses, the date would be announced by the respective course coordinators. A student can appear for a maximum of three such additional tests in a given semester. If a student cannot appear for the test due to any reason(s), he/she will not get any additional chance. If a student with ‘E’ grade in a course does not pass the course through the additional test, or obtains an ‘F’ grade in the course, he/she has to repeat the course if it is a core course. In case the course is elective, the student may take the same course again or any other course. ‘E’ and ‘F’ Grades are not counted in the calculation of the CGPA; however, these are taken into account in the calculation of the SGPA. 3 I An ‘I’ grade is temporarily awarded to a student on his/her request to denote incomplete performance in a course on approval of instructor. An ‘I’ grade is awarded in case missing an evaluation component due to absence on medical grounds or other special circumstances. Requests for ‘I’ grade should be made at the earliest but not later than the last day of major tests. All evaluation requirements for such students in the corresponding course(s) should be completed before the end of the first week of the next semester. Upon completion of all course requirements, the ‘I’ grade is converted to a regular grade. 4 S This grade is awarded to a student with satisfactory performance in non-graded and Audit courses. If the stipulated requirements are not fulfilled, the unsatisfactory (U) grade is awarded. The grades obtained in an audit course are not considered in the calculation of SGPA or CGPA. 5 X This grade is awarded to a student with satisfactory performance in thesis for continuation 6 U This grade is awarded to a student with unsatisfactory performance in thesis, audit or non-graded courses. 7 W This grade is awarded to a student who has opted to withdraw from a course. If the grade points associated with the letter grades earned by a student in N courses registered during a semester are G ​ 1 ​ , G ​ 2 ​ , … G ​ N ​ , and the corresponding credits C ​ 1 ​ , C ​ 2 ​ , … C ​ N ​ , then the SGPA is given by the following formula: The SGPA is calculated on the basis of grades obtained in all courses, except audit courses and courses in which S/X grade is awarded, registered in a particular semester. 5.3.2 Cumulative Grade Point Average The Cumulative Grade Point Average (CGPA) indicates the overall academic performance of a student in all the courses registered up to the latest completed semester. 8. MAKE-UP EXAMINATIONS A student who has missed minor(s) or the major examination due to genuine reasons like illness etc. may be permitted to write a make-up examination for the missed components. The student should make an application to the Dean (Academics) through the course instructor within ten days from the date of the examination missed, explaining the reasons for their absence. Applications received after this period need not be entertained. The permission to take a make-up examination will be given under exceptional circumstances such as admission to a hospital due to illness. A student needs to produce the necessary document subject to one of the following categories: ● Students residing in the Hostels should produce a Medical Certificate issued by the Medical Officer of the Institute that he/she was admitted to the Hospital during the period of the missed quiz/exam. ● Students residing in the Hostels and taking medical consultation with outside Doctors are required to obtain written permission from the Medical Officer of the Institute Hospital before they proceed for such consultation. ● Students residing in the hostels but taking medical consultation with outside Doctors are required to obtain an endorsement on the certificate of treatment by the Medical Officer of the Institute Hospital. ● A student staying outside the Campus permanently / temporarily must produce a medical certificate from the Registered Medical Practitioner and the same should be duly endorsed by the parent/guardian. A slot-wise make-up examination for major will be held during the makeup / supplementary week as per Academic Calendar of the subsequent semester for those who are permitted to take the make-up examination. A student who misses this make-up examination will not normally be given another make-up examination. However, in exceptional cases of prolonged illness resulting in the student missing a make-up examination, the Chairman of the Senate, in consultation with the Dean of Academics may permit the student to appear for make-up examination any day before the end of the first week of the next semester. Under no circumstances, prorating can be done for the missed examinations or attendance. 11

9. UNDERGRADUATE PROGRAMMES IIT Jodhpur currently offers Bachelor of Technology (B. Tech.) programs, and capability linked opportunities for undergraduate students to complete Minor/Interdisciplinary Area Specializations or Department Area Specialization. A student can also opt for M.Tech.(dual degree) in Departmental Area or Minor in Entrepreneurship leading to M.Tech. in Entrepreneurship or Department Area Specialization in Engineering innovation. 10. UNDERGRADUATE ADMISSIONS 10.1 B.Tech. Programmes 10.1.1 General Admissions Admissions to the B.Tech. Programmes are made once a year in July through the all-India level Joint Entrance Examination (JEE) conducted by IITs. The procedures and other requirements for admission are specified in the JEE Information Brochure brought out every year. 10.1.2 Cultural Exchange Programmes Admissions are also offered to foreign nationals under the Cultural Exchange Fellowship Program of the Government of India, administered by Indian Council of Cultural Relations (ICCR), New Delhi.
